title: 'One of the greats' signs off after fourth Roosters premiership
text:
Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson has hailed Daniel Tupou as one of the NRL club's all-time greats after the four-time premiership-winning winger announced his retirement.

Tupou is ending his 15-year career on a high after helping the Roosters win Sunday's grand final against Newcastle.

The 35-year-old, who had been coy about his future all season, became just the sixth player in Roosters history to win four premierships with the club.

Across a 307-game, one-club career, the winger scored 198 tries, the third most of any player in premiership history behind Ken Irvine and Alex Johnston.

"When you look at what Daniel Tupou has achieved over 15 seasons, he will stand as one of the greats," Robinson said in a statement.

"But those numbers only tell part of the story of Toops and what he means to this club.

Tupou a Roosters grand final specialist Daniel Tupou is edging closer to becoming the first Roosters player in more than 80 years to win four premierships because he always finds his best on the biggest day of the season.

"Since he made his debut, he has represented what we want a Rooster to be.

"He has been incredibly consistent, selfless and dependable, and whenever there has been a big moment or a tough moment, he has been present.

"Toops revolutionised the aerial game at the Sydney Roosters and became the greatest high-ball specialist of all time."

Tupou's exit comes as the Roosters prepare for a big off-season exodus over the coming weeks.

Fellow winger Mark Nawaqanitawase and second rower Angus Crichton are moving to rugby union, playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans is heading to Super League side Hull FC, and Connor Watson is joining St George Illawarra.

But none of them gets close to having the impact the towering winger has had on the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2012.

As well as four premierships (2013, 2018, 2019, 2026), Tupou has won three World Club Challenges and played Test matches for both Tonga and Australia.

He was part of the Tongan side that defeated the Kangaroos in 2019 in one of the biggest upsets in international rugby league history.

Tupou played 10 times for NSW at State of Origin level between 2014 and 2022.

"We love Toops, we're incredibly proud of him, and his name will always hold a very special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters," Robinson said.

Tupou retires as the greatest try-scorer in Roosters history after surpassing Anthony Minichiello in 2023.

title: Volunteer ambulance officer of almost 50 years stood down amid investigation
text:
Volunteer ambulance officers in a country South Australian town have walked out in protest at one of their peers being stood down, raising concerns about the local service's future.

Pinnaroo local and volunteer Rob Berlin was stood down last week after giving his time to the South Australian Ambulance Service (SAAS) for almost 50 years.

Some volunteer members of the local service, based 240 kilometres east of Adelaide and servicing a population of about 760 people, have made themselves unavailable for rostering in support.

Volunteers are central to the operation of the SA Ambulance Service's Pinnaroo Station. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce )

The ABC has made several attempts to contact Mr Berlin, but he has not responded.

An anonymous social media post, which has been circulated widely, detailed the allegations against Mr Berlin, describing them as "administrative" and criticising SAAS's action.

An SAAS spokesperson said while they were aware of the concerns that have been raised publicly, information circulating online does not reflect the facts of the situation.

They said they were unable to comment on confidential individual matters.

"However, we are committed to ensuring any allegations are investigated fairly and in accordance with our rigorous policies and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The service situation

The Pinnaroo ambulance station relies on volunteers to operate and they work closely alongside the Lameroo station, which is about 40 kilometres away.

Collectively the two stations respond to fewer than 10 jobs a week on average, SAAS said.

The Pinnaroo ambulance station is staffed entirely by volunteers. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

Southern Mallee District Council mayor Ron Valentine said he had met with community members and the local state member of parliament about the ambulance station and its operation in recent days.

He said various community members had questioned the "legitimacy and transparency" of the allegations when speaking with him.

Cr Valentine said other ambulance volunteers had told him they had also decided to not make themselves available to be rostered in support of Mr Berlin, and would only return if the state government committed to an independent investigation into the dispute.

"In my view, you can't have a truly independent investigation if you're part of the issue," Cr Valentine said.

" One of the problems is as volunteers, they don't really have any representation. There's no union standing up for them. "

Vital volunteers

MacKillop MP Jason Virgo said he would write to the relevant minister asking for an independent investigation to be established after meeting Pinnaroo locals.

Jason Virgo met with the local community last week to discuss the issue. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

He said the largest challenge is that volunteers are difficult to find.

"If you've got Pinnaroo down in terms of volunteers, and if they're not feeling heard, the concern is that … the feeling might get out there in the community and we might not be able to replace them either," Mr Virgo said.

"If Lameroo is understaffed and can't help Pinnaroo or if Pinnaroo's got no volunteers, then the closest you're going to is the Riverland or south to Bordertown through black spots."

The SA Ambulance spokesperson said the organisation had put in arrangements to support local coverage while volunteer availability was down, including bringing on an additional volunteer from outside the town.

"We can reassure the community we are strongly committed to providing Pinnaroo with ongoing ambulance services and upholding the highest standards for the benefit of the community," the spokesperson said.

title: Woolworths freight fuel levy surcharge almost triples since Iran war
text:
Woolworths has increased the fuel levy charged through its logistics network to food and grocery suppliers to almost triple its pre-Iran war level as diesel costs continue to climb.

The fuel levy surcharges have increased for metro and regional areas, affecting some of the country's largest food and grocery manufacturers.

This includes Primary Connect, Woolworths' logistics arm, which transports goods from suppliers to distribution centres and stores across the country.

The business manages freight for more than 1,000 grocery producers, including brands such as Sanitarium, PepsiCo, Ingham's and Arnott's.

The fuel levy for metro areas recently rose from 17.47 per cent to 19.88 per cent.

In regional Australia, the levy increased from 44.20 per cent to 50.30 per cent.

University of Sydney supply chain management professor Rico Merkert said the increases were not unusual when diesel prices rose sharply.

"Fuel levies are commonly used in freight markets to manage fuel-price volatility," Professor Merkert said.

"Many transport operators use surcharges that can be adjusted periodically rather than renegotiating contracts every time fuel costs move.

"If diesel costs rise sharply, it is economically reasonable for freight providers and retailers to increase fuel surcharges to recover those additional operating costs."

Rico Merkert says transport costs are only one component of the final retail price at the supermarket. (Supplied)

Prior to the Iran war, the fuel levy Woolworths charged in metro areas was 7.28 per cent.

Within weeks of the war, it had risen to 12.47 per cent.

The regional fuel levy has jumped by more than 172 per cent since March, when it was 18.44 per cent.

Consumers likely to feel impact

Experts believe the increase in freight costs are likely to be shared across the supply chain.

"My prediction is that consumers and suppliers will get the worst end of the deal of the fuel surcharge increase," said Medo Pournader, senior lecturer of supply chain management at the University of Melbourne.

University of Sydney professor Ben Fahimnia, who is also a specialist on the issue, said continually pushing rising logistics costs back onto suppliers is not a sustainable solution.

"They have absorbed some of the costs initially and have tried to find savings elsewhere, but there is a limit to what businesses can absorb," Professor Fahimnia said.

" Someone ultimately has to pay, and, at these fuel levy rates, that will be Australian consumers at the check-out. "

While Professor Merkert agrees, he believes the effect is unlikely to be one-for-one.

"Higher fuel levies can eventually contribute to higher retail prices and hence inflation, but freight is only one element of the final shelf price, so consumers would not necessarily see a direct or proportional increase at the check-out," he said.

Rising fuel prices have played a significant part in Australia's inflation rate, which recently jumped to 4 per cent in August.

Transport was the second-largest contributor to the annual inflation figure as a result of higher automotive fuel prices.

Inflation lower than expected The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected, with headline inflation up 4 per cent in the year to August.

On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 14.8 per cent in August, compared with a rise of 7.5 per cent in July.

In a press conference after last week's monetary policy decision, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned businesses were preparing to pass on higher fuel costs if necessary.

"The longer it [the war] lasts, if businesses were thinking, "Oh, look, it'll come off, I won't pass on costs," the longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases," Ms Bullock said.

title: Logan mayor warns of backyard 'slums' as council slashes granny flat tax
text:
Granny flats will be $13,500 cheaper to build in Logan after controversial new rules were passed by Logan City Council today.

The council voted to halve its $27,000 infrastructure charge for one-bedroom secondary dwellings to incentivise new granny flats.

Logan Mayor Jon Raven opposed the move, saying it would be exploited by landlords to fit more renters onto small backyard lots.

He blamed laws introduced by the Queensland government in 2022 that allowed property owners to rent granny flats to non-family members.

Jon Raven says granny flats should be for families, not property investors. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Cr Raven said this was a "loophole" which allowed property investors to build more developments than they would otherwise be allowed to build.

He said Logan's previous attempts to incentivise more secondary dwellings caused severe suburban overcrowding due to these laws.

"We saw what happened with auxiliary units where you could put a two-bedroom secondary dwelling on the same site as a three-bedroom primary dwelling," Cr Raven said.

"We got slums, and we can still see them in parts of the city today, because we can't remove them once they've been approved.

"Savvy investors will find a way to exploit the discount as best as possible."

Doing the right thing

Councillor Nathan St Ledger supported the move, saying more families wanted to move in together due to the growing unaffordability of housing.

He said council's charges were "bloody expensive" and preventing more granny flats from being built.

He said this would bolster the supply of affordable housing in Logan, even if much of it was run by unscrupulous property investors.

"You've got rocks in your head if you think people aren't going to do it," Cr St Ledger said.

"I completely understand the problem it could cause … but what about the residents who want to do the right thing?"

Under Logan's current rules, infrastructure charges can be waived entirely if the granny flat is connected to the primary house and is used for family members.

The changes are expected to commence in November this year.

The motion passed with the support of eight councillors, with three opposing and one abstaining.

The councillors who opposed were Mindy Rusell, Paul Jackson, and Cr Raven, with Teresa Lane abstaining.

title: Marrickville Golf Club received closed non-competitive grants on five past occasions
text:
Marrickville Golf Club received closed, non-competitive grant funding on five previous occasions before the Albanese government awarded it $6 million for a major redevelopment of its clubhouse, stormwater systems and grounds.

The club was handed $21,450 in funding in 2019-20 for a toilet and locker room upgrade, $11,000 in 2021 to upgrade its computer operating system and $12,650 in 2021-22 to install energy-saving downlights at the clubhouse.

It also received $3,410 in 2022 to plant rows of flame trees and install a plaque to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee, and a further $9,350 that year to install benches around the golf course.

In total, it received $57,860 in closed funding across the five federal grants.

While three of those grants were awarded under the former Coalition government, in each case the local member of parliament was asked to identify projects worthy of financial support.

The Sydney suburb of Marrickville was previously split across the federal seats of Grayndler, held by Anthony Albanese and Barton, held by Linda Burney.

The golf club itself was in Ms Burney's seat at the time the five grants were awarded.

Mr Albanese and Ms Burney were both involved in a 2020 campaign to save the course being cut from 18 holes down to nine holes, a proposal that was ultimately defeated.

Anthony Albanese and Linda Burney both joined a campaign to "save Marrickville Golf Club from developers". (Instagram: Darcy Byrne)

The ABC revealed last month that Mr Albanese held an undisclosed honorary membership to Marrickville Golf Club, which he promised $6 million at the federal election in 2025, and with which he has a decades-long association.

The prime minister has dismissed concerns, saying he was not aware of the membership.

"I don't have a card, I don't go in there, I haven't been in there for years," Mr Albanese told the ABC last month.

Albanese held undeclared honorary membership to golf club given $6m Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held an honorary membership to the Marrickville Golf Club in his seat, which was promised $6 million at the 2025 election through an invite-only scheme, and which Mr Albanese has not declared.

Constitutional lawyer Anne Twomey identified the past grants in a submission to an inquiry into the Major Local Community Infrastructure (MLCI) grants scheme, under which the $6 million in funding was awarded.

"What is remarkable is that all these grants were classified as 'closed, non-competitive,'" Professor Twomey wrote.

"The effect was that the Marrickville Golf Club was granted funds without any assessment of whether it had greater need for these grants than anyone else. They were effectively gifts of political largesse, funded by taxpayers."

Mr Albanese also previously promised $340,000 for the club at the 2016 election for a new verandah and function space, and again promised $350,000 at the 2019 election to deliver those same upgrades.

That funding was not awarded because Labor did not win the 2016 or 2019 elections.

Anthony Albanese previously promised Marrickville Golf Club hundreds of thousands of dollars in funding at two federal elections. (X: Anthony Albanese)

PM's sewage fix disputed

Following reports of his membership, Mr Albanese defended the $6 million grant in Question Time, saying it had been awarded to stop raw sewage from flowing across the golf course and into nearby Cooks River.

But in her submission, Professor Twomey questioned the prime minister's claim the funding was to upgrade the club's sewage system, noting that his initial media release did not refer to that but rather clubhouse renovations, stormwater harvesting upgrades to irrigate the golf course and outdoor upgrades.

"There was no reference to the more recent claim that the money is to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the Cooks River," she wrote.

Professor Twomey said those sewage fixes were actually being done under another grant given to the Marrickville Golf Club, a $269,500 NSW government grant awarded in 2025 to connect the clubhouse to the sewer, and avoid the use of septic tanks that were overflowing during floods.

The ABC has identified at least two other state grants awarded to the Marrickville Golf Club, a $35,000 grant in 2021 to install solar panels on the club roof, and $8,000 that same year for watering system maintenance.

Jo Haylen hands a cheque to the Marrickville Golf Club to install solar panels on its club roof. (Facebook: Jo Haylen)

Summer Hill MP Jo Haylen celebrated both grants with giant cheques to the club, which was also where Ms Haylen launched her campaign for state parliament in 2015 alongside Mr Albanese.

Jo Haylen hands a cheque for water system maintenance to the Marrickville Golf Club. (Facebook: Jo Haylen)

Professor Twomey said in this case the Major and Local Community Infrastructure program did appear to be constitutional, although an earlier version of it may not have been.

But she noted that closed non-competitive grants like those awarded under the MLCI appeared "incompatible" with grant rules, since they did not have a proper selection process or "genuine assessment" of merit or value for money, as required.

"It is hard to see how a Minister, in approving grants, can genuinely be satisfied that the expenditure is efficient, effective, economical and ethical in such circumstances," Professor Twomey wrote.

"The system is a farce, with the paperwork drafted to justify decisions already made without any consideration of merit, need, value for money or the public interest."

The Infrastructure Department confirmed in its submission to the inquiry that projects had been chosen by Labor, with no oversight by the department.

"The department had no role in identifying, selecting or recommending projects or applicants invited to apply under the program, nor determining project funding value," it wrote.

"The department did not provide any advice to government in relation to identifying, selecting or recommending applicants invited to apply at any point, and the government did not seek any such advice from the department. This includes the geographic distribution of projects."

A senate inquiry is seeking to examine how projects were identified for MLCI funding and whether there were any perceived or actual conflicts on interest in grants being nominated.

A Centre for Public Integrity examination of the program found funding flowed overwhelmingly to seats favouring Labor, which prompted accusations the government used public money to pork barrel at the 2025 election.

Professor Twomey said election grants schemes were a form of "grey corruption", where governments excise power for private or political interests over the national interest.

"Federal politicians should not be making election promises about specific local projects and should not be making promises for the spending of public money based on political self interest rather than the public interest," Professor Twomey said.

"This is not about 'being a good local Member'. It is about indulging in grey corruption and the misuse of public money at the public’s expense."

title: Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc after RBA card surcharge ban
text:
A ban on card surcharges has resulted in some cafe owners raising the price of their coffee.

About 17 per cent of cafes are now charging more for a flat white, compared with prices prior to October 1, when the Reserve Bank's ban took effect.

That is according to Small Flat White, an online platform that tracks coffee prices across more than 1,500 cafes.

Typically, the increase was 50 cents, or almost 10 per cent of the coffee's price, which is much higher than the typical 0.5 to 1.5 per cent surcharge consumers used to pay on their credit or debit card transactions.

Avtar Singh says most small businesses are operating on thin margins. (ABC News)

Not every hospitality business has raised its prices in the immediate aftermath of the ban.

Avtar Singh, owner of a Thai restaurant in Hobart, said he was currently absorbing the cost of the surcharges but eventually would have to raise prices.

"The government needs to understand small businesses are already at a very thin margin," he told the ABC.

"If you squeeze it any further, it'll come to a point where doing business is very, very difficult."

RBA kicks 'own goal'

Wes Lambert says the card surcharge ban has led to unintended results. (ABC News)

Most cafes or restaurants have raised prices in some way, either by raising menu prices or increasing weekend or public holiday surcharges, said Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association.

"Increasing prices can always affect demand, so that certainly is an unintended consequence that the RBA could not have predicted, because they believed that prices would only go up 0.1 per cent," he said.

Mr Lambert said some businesses had started taking cash-only payments or accepting bank transfers.

"Ultimately, we think that the RBA kicked an own goal in this," he added.

"They should have known better that inflation was going to remain pesky and that this ban would come online during a cost of living crisis and potentially should have delayed the ban during this high inflationary and high interest environment."

The RBA has said the previous system was no longer working as intended, with surcharges increasingly difficult for consumers to avoid.

The central bank has also said only about 16 per cent of businesses were surcharging and the ban was designed to reduce card acceptance costs, particularly for small businesses.

Reforms unlikely to affect interest rates

Luci Ellis says the changes will not have a significant impact on inflation. (ABC News)

If the surcharge ban results in higher inflation, that effect would likely be temporary and have no effect on interest rates, according to Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis.

"Previously surcharges were imposed to reflect the cost of accepting certain types of payment; that's now been bundled into the price, so some business have increased their prices, but that's a one-off, not inherently inflationary," she said.

"Most of the reports we've seen of prices increasing … more than what the surcharge had been were in hospitality.

"There are plenty of other inflationary forces going round, including the pass-through of high energy costs onto other prices that the Reserve Bank's going to be much more focused on."

New surcharge ban Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed.

"The overall macroeconomic impact from higher prices flowing from the ban on surcharges may not be that significant," he said.

Mr Oliver said many large businesses were already not charging surcharges.

"It's really just an issue for small businesses, but there still may be some upwards boost to inflation, albeit minor," he said.

"In theory, the RBA may just look through it as it's a one-off impact, but it may be hard to disentangle a general rise in prices from the impact of the surcharge versus other factors."

The Reserve Bank declined to comment.

title: What Paramount's Warner Bros takeover means for what we watch
text:
Paramount has completed its $US113 billion ($162 billion) takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating one of the world's biggest entertainment and media companies.

The new company will be led by David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, whose family has close ties with US President Donald Trump.

The mega-merger brings some of Hollywood's biggest film, television and news brands under one roof, from The Godfather, Top Gun and Star Trek to Harry Potter, Friends, Game of Thrones and the DC universe.

For audiences, it means an enormous catalogue of movies and television shows is controlled by one company.

David Ellison says the settlement represents "complete clearance" for the merger. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

It also brings together two businesses already serving Australian audiences, with Paramount's Network 10 and Paramount+ joining Warner Bros Discovery's HBO Max.

But for Hollywood and the wider media industry, there are concerns about what happens when fewer companies control more of the entertainment and news we consume.

Just how big is the new company?

Paramount Skydance is now a huge player in movies, television, streaming and news.

Its stable includes Mission: Impossible, Top Gun, Star Trek, SpongeBob SquarePants, South Park and The Godfather.

Warner Bros Discovery brings Harry Potter, Friends, Game of Thrones, The Last of Us, The Big Bang Theory, Succession, The White Lotus and the DC universe.

Then there's HBO, Warner Bros Television, CNN and CBS, alongside Australia's Network 10.

Warner Bros Discovery includes Game of Thrones. (HBO)

The deal also reshapes Hollywood's traditional studio landscape, combining two of the five major legacy studios, Paramount and Warner Bros, leaving Disney, Universal Pictures and Sony Pictures as the other three.

David Folkenflik is a media correspondent with NPR and author of Murdoch's World: The Last of the Old Media Empires.

"It's an extraordinary moment for Hollywood and for the media writ large, and it's a moment for corporates and conglomeration as well," Mr Folkenflik said.

"You have these two proud Hollywood titles, Paramount Pictures, Warner Brothers Studios under the same roof, you now have CBS News and CNN under the same roof, you have Star Trek and DC Comics under the same roof."

Loading...

Why are people in Hollywood worried?

The merger comes at a difficult time for the entertainment industry.

Traditional studios are competing with global streaming services, while production costs are rising and audiences are increasingly watching content online.

The new company is also carrying significant debt and has committed to major cost savings.

Hollywood journalist Kim Masters, a former editor-at-large at The Hollywood Reporter, said the company was under significant financial pressure.

"This company is absolutely strapped with debt and needs to, according to the agreement with their lenders, they need to do some things very quickly to get things in shape," Ms Masters said.

"And so therefore, Hollywood is cringing in terms of those lay-offs."

Paramount takes over Warner Bros The combined company, Skydance, brings together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures, the CBS News and CNN networks, and the HBO and CBS TV brands

She also said the merger left filmmakers with fewer major studios to approach for funding.

"So we're pretty much down to … Universal, Sony, Apple, but we don't know to what extent Apple is really interested in doing movies," she said.

"You know, it's just a loss of potentially two studio buyers for that kind of product."

And she said that could make it harder for directors working on films without an obvious commercial appeal to find backing.

"I think it's going to be more difficult for our auteur directors to find that kind of backing," she said.

Does a bigger library mean more choice?

The merger brings together a huge amount of existing content.

But the issue for Hollywood isn't simply how many movies and shows are available. It's how many companies are left deciding what gets made, funded, promoted and distributed.

Professor Matthew Ricketson from Deakin University said the bigger issue was the concentration of media ownership itself.

"Diversity of views, plurality of views and stories … if there is a lack of diversity of them … that is absolutely not a good thing," he said.

What could it mean for streaming prices?

The merger also brings together Paramount+ and HBO Max under the same corporate ownership.

David Folkenflik said consumers would bear some of the cost of the new company's debt.

"It's hard to believe those prices won't go up. I think the consumers are going to be hit," he said.

The company is targeting about $US6 billion a year in savings, and Folkenflik said those savings were likely to come from both staffing and content.

He said that could affect what audiences were ultimately offered.

"And that means that, you know, prices could potentially ramp up and you could see a diminishment of the combined amount of things offered," he said.

And then there's the news

The merger is significant because Paramount Skydance isn't only an entertainment company.

It also has major news interests, including CBS News and CNN, while its Australian operations include Network 10.

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday local time he was a strong supporter of the merger.

"That's great. It's gonna be a great company. They're terrific people and it's going to be a great company," Mr Trump said.

The new owner, David Ellison, is the son of Oracle co-founder and billionaire Larry Ellison, whose family has developed close ties with Mr Trump.

Paramount clears way for Warner Bros merger Opponents say Paramount's multi-billion-dollar merger with Warner Bros will slash Hollywood jobs, reduce the number of films produced, and threaten CNN's independence.

Mr Folkenflik said that relationship was one of the key questions surrounding the takeover.

"I think that's the real question for journalists, and I think it probably is a question for a lot of their audiences at CBS and CNN," he said.

Professor Ricketson said the significance of the merger extended beyond the entertainment industry.

"Skydance will now control two of the five news outlets that currently constitute the pool at the White House, that is CBS News and CNN," he said.

CNN has been in a dispute with the Trump administration over access to the White House, with the network challenging restrictions in court.

Professor Ricketson said the relationship between the new ownership and the Trump administration raised serious questions about editorial independence.

"We've already seen those efforts by the Trump administration trying to kick out of the White House, the access to the White House of CNN, and two other news organisations. And saying they're doing that on the grounds that those outlets are lying or spreading fake news," he said.

He said the issue went to the heart of the relationship between political power and news organisations.

"We've already seen that Donald Trump's idea of favourable coverage is that you say wonderful things about me, terrible things about my opponents. And if you say anything other than that, you are either fake news or you are a hoax or you are lying when in fact, that's absolutely not been the case," he said.

Mr Ellison has said CNN would remain an independent newsroom, with Mark Thompson continuing as its editor-in-chief.

Professor Ricketson said the fundamental question was who got to decide what constituted legitimate reporting.

"Who is determining what are the lies here and who is determining what is the fake news?"

What does it mean for Australians?

For most Australians, there probably won't be an immediate dramatic change.

But two streaming services Australians already use, Paramount+ and HBO Max, are now owned by the same company and are expected to eventually be combined.

It has not yet been announced what the new service will look like, what content it will include or how much it will cost.

Network 10 also gives Skydance a significant presence in the Australian media market, with the company now behind programs including MasterChef Australia, Australian Survivor and 10 News.

title: 'Looking at Australia': Sidney Nolan in six definitive paintings
text:
Australian artist Sidney Nolan was interested in the stories and myths we tell about ourselves, from the life of bushranger Ned Kelly to the trials of saints.

"Sidney Nolan has to be one of our most creative and inventive painters that emerged out of the period of war and the decades following," says Denise Mimmocchi, senior curator of Australian art at the Art Gallery of New South Wales (AGNSW).

"He posed questions about place, our identity, and our individual search for meaning within the continent and landscapes of Australia."

Born in 1917, the modernist artist would prove to be one of Australia's most influential and prolific, initially as part of the infamous Heide Circle alongside Albert Tucker, Arthur Boyd and Joy Hester. He would go on to be acquired by the likes of the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate Modern in London.

Sidney Nolan in 1954, photographed by fellow artist Albert Tucker. Nolan died in 1992. (Supplied: State Library of Victoria)

Curated by Mimmocchi, AGNSW's new exhibition Nolan: Origins charts the artist's career from 1939 until he moved to London in 1953. It features places like St Kilda and central Australia — environments that would continue to spark his imagination throughout his life.

"I wanted to look at what inspired him," Mimmocchi says. "And what we're looking at really is Australia."

Kiata

In 1943, during WWII, Nolan — who had been conscripted in 1942 — was stationed at Nhill, guarding Australia's food reserves.

The job left him with a lot of time to paint. One work he made during this period is this landscape of the nearby town Kiata, in western Victoria.

"Kiata is really a breakthrough moment," Mimmocchi says. "This is when the abstract artist also becomes a landscape painter."

In Kiata, you can see a precursor to the shape of his Ned Kelly helmet in the horse-drawn wagon. (Supplied: AGNSW)

As he figured out how to capture the vastness he encountered, Nolan came to appreciate an earlier generation of Australian artists, the Impressionists, like Arthur Streeton, Tom Roberts and Charles Conder, who would often paint outdoors.

"He looks to and echoes in his own way the idea of painting the Australian light and landscape, but he does it through his own modern sensibility," Mimmocchi says.

A year later, in 1944, when he found out he was going to be sent to fight in Papua New Guinea, Nolan deserted the army.

In 1948, he received an amnesty for deserters and was formally discharged.

Fire, Palais de Danse, St Kilda

When Nolan was nine and growing up in Melbourne's St Kilda, the Palais de Danse burned down. It was an event that became etched in the artist's memory.

He painted the scene 20 years later, in 1945, while living between his studio in Parkville, Melbourne, and Heide on the city's outskirts, in the home of philanthropists Sunday and John Reed.

There, Nolan had an affair with Sunday, before marrying John's sister, Cynthia, a writer, in 1948.

"When he's living in hiding, he starts to paint with greater intensity these memories of his childhood in St Kilda," Mimmocchi says.

"He goes up in scale as well. In that expansion comes this incredible impact of the energy contained within them."

When Nolan was a boy, he noticed energy "streaming through at an enormous rate". (Supplied: AGNSW)

She describes that energy as "frenetic", with the human figures in the painting appearing almost like ants.

"You get this sense of palpitating movement," Mimmocchi explains. "It's wonderful and vibrant but at the same time, for me, a little tense. There's something deeply anxious about them."

Mimmocchi boils that anxiety down to Nolan viewing these moments from his childhood through the lens of the "wartime present".

Ned Kelly

While living at Heide, Nolan spent a year, starting in 1946, creating a series of 27 paintings of bushranger Ned Kelly.

All 27 paintings in Sidney Nolan's Ned Kelly series are on display at AGNSW. (Supplied: NGA)

One inspiration for the series came from the stories Nolan's grandfather told him when he was a child, of being part of the search for the Kelly gang. But it also stemmed from his own desertion from the army.

"He's a bit of an outlaw in his mind himself," Mimmocchi says.

"He saw the Kelly figure as a rebel poet. He saw him and his family as the victims of great injustice.

"At the same time, coming out of that experience of war, where he was trained to use the 'utmost violence', the idea of brutality was at the forefront of his mind."

To create the series, Nolan pored over newspaper clippings and the 1881 Royal Commission report into the Victorian police, and visited Glenrowan, the site of Kelly's final shoot-out with police in 1880.

"He's interested in painting the landscape and the stories within it; how history becomes legend becomes mythology," Mimmocchi says.

That's perhaps exemplified by the view through the letterbox-style slit in Kelly's helmet.

"We view the landscape through the Kelly helmet," Mimmocchi says. "It's almost as if Nolan is saying our experiences of place are shaped or framed by these stories, by these figures."

The Ned Kelly series and the now-iconic blocky shape of Kelly's helmet also marked a turning point in Nolan's practice.

"He said he was an abstract painter and then he became a painter of the landscape, and this brought the two together," Mimmocchi says.

Quilting the armour

This 1947 painting from the Ned Kelly series depicts a moment of tenderness between the bushranger and his sister Margaret, where she stitched padding into his helmet.

Nolan described the Ned Kelly series as a "post-war meditation on violence". (Supplied: AGNSW)

"It's quite a beautiful and powerful image of this woman creating padding for Kelly in this foreboding landscape, perhaps in anticipation of the violence which is to come," Mimmocchi says.

"It sits so distinctly from a lot of the other paintings, which are about the guns, the violence, the bloodshed.

"It says something about a female notion of creativity or the importance of women in the Ned Kelly story."

Forensic imaging reveals hidden layers under Ned Kelly paintings Hidden figures and inscriptions are being discovered beneath some of Australia's most famous paintings as conservators use infrared technology to reveal details in Sidney Nolan's Ned Kelly series.

Also hidden in the painting is a reference to Nolan's desertion from the army, living under the alias Robin Murray. On a fencepost sits a red robin.

The Ned Kelly series fell flat when it was first exhibited in Melbourne in 1948, but the Reeds were determined the paintings would find an audience, sending them to Paris and Rome.

In Paris in 1949, museum director Jean Cassou described them as "the work of a true poet and true painter".

"It wasn't until they'd had this life overseas that they came back to Australia and started to gain the recognition they deserve," Mimmocchi says.

Central Australia

In 1949, Nolan spent months travelling through central Australia, Arnhem Land and the Kimberley in Western Australia, with his wife, Cynthia, and adopted daughter Jinx.

"[Central Australia] is such a superb and sublime vision of place," Mimmocchi says. (Supplied: AGNSW)

The artist would join aviator Eddie Connellan as he delivered mail to remote communities. The view from these flights inspired this 1950 painting.

"He was deeply inspired by this vision of a country, which was so vast, so seemingly infinite, but had this vital energy in the movement and passages of the landscape," Mimmocchi says.

"It was painted at a time when city Australians commonly referred to the centre of Australia as its dead heart. Nolan encounters and paints a country that couldn't be more different to that."

The vivid red of the work comes from Nolan's use of Ripolin, a quick-drying enamel paint he first used in the early 40s.

"That gave him a saturated colour and the ability to paint the intense, clarified light of the desert," Mimmocchi says.

In 1950, in a letter to fellow artist Albert Tucker, Nolan wrote that Indigenous peoples "show you that the country is a gentle, dreaming one; the barrenness and harshness is all in our European eyes".

Mimmocchi explains: "First Nations connection to Country shaped his vision."

Temptation of St Anthony

In 1950, Nolan travelled to Europe for the first time, to Italy, Spain, Greece and the UK, where he was inspired by Christian paintings.

When he returned to Sydney, he started taking biblical scenes and imposing them onto the unforgiving Australian landscape.

Mimmocchi describes Temptation of St Anthony as "wonderfully wacky". (Supplied: AGNSW)

In Temptation of St Anthony, from 1952, he depicted the story of early Christian monk Anthony the Great's pilgrimage through the Egyptian desert, where he was tormented by demons and faced a series of temptations.

In Nolan's telling, those demons and temptations included a goanna, a giant dragonfly and an angel with horns.

"He was deeply interested in the stories that shape us," Mimmocchi says. "It was the idea of myth. He saw the stories of the Bible as another myth that could be painted in relation to the landscape.

"In these biblical works, he's marrying this sense of the ancientness of the stories of Europe with the ancientness and the vital presence of the Australian landscape."

For the curator, Temptation of St Anthony is "pure Nolan".

"He's able to bring the action of this biblical story into the Australian desert so evocatively," she says.

Nolan: Origins is at Art Gallery of New South Wales, Sydney, until February 7.

title: Lionel Messi scores final goal in emotional farewell to Argentina
text:
Lionel Messi has delivered one last masterclass in blue and white as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international ​career by scoring a goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium was less about football ​and more a national ‌celebration of Messi's service to Argentina.

Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team's sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans ‌poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem.

Messi's family watched proudly ⁠from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of ‌1978, 1986 and 2022.

"Even through the worst moments we went through, I never stopped fighting, battling, giving everything I had, wanting to always be here," Messi told the crowd after full-time.

Lionel Messi was emotional as he signed off from international duty. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

"I love all of you, and I will miss all of you. I am proud to be Argentine."

Hours earlier, a ​massive number 10 shirt ‌emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's home town.

As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route.

When the teams took the pitch, Benin captain Sessi D'Almeida looked lost ​for ‌words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake.

The crowd rose for applause and more fireworks erupted in the stadium as the clock ticked past the 10th minute of the match.

After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home ⁠Argentina's opener.

Otamendi shared 17 years with ‌Messi in the national team, including ‌four World Cups, and was also ending his international career.

Messi then set up Nico Paz, one ‌of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's number 10 shirt, to score the second goal.

In a fairytale ending, Messi converted ‌a penalty ​for 3-0, his 126th ⁠international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd.

At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent ⁠Argentina career.

Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international ‌stage into a ‌story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.

For years, Argentina asked ​Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say thank you.

Reuters

title: Farming family's trusted bookkeeper jailed for $2.8m fraud
text:
A disgraced bookkeeper has been jailed for 12 years for defrauding almost $2.8 million from the farming family that employed her for almost two decades.

Michelle Kathleen Lawson, 53, systematically abused her trusted position to steal money from businesses belonging to the Johnston family of Tully in Far North Queensland between 2017 and 2023.

Lawson disguised her fraud as wage payments to fictitious employees and through false invoices, the District Court in Cairns heard.

Lawson, who was caught after a tax agent found discrepancies in accounting records, used $2.5 million to fund what Judge Joshua Treviño KC described as an "extremely lavish lifestyle".

Michelle Lawson worked for the Johnstons, a long-standing Tully farming family, for 18 years. (ABC Rural: Melanie Groves)

She used the Johnstons' money to pay for horses, education for her children, personal insurance bills, travel and accommodation.

"Your extravagance included spending almost $1 million of the money you stole on retail expenditure," Judge Treviño said.

" A quarter of a million of that sum on clothing and shoes alone. "

A forensic investigation could not account for $300,000 but the court heard Lawson accepted she used the Johnstons' money to buy into a clothing boutique.

Lawson worked in Tully and once served as treasurer of the town's business chamber. (ABC News: Dominic Cansdale)

"The use of funds for that purpose really underlines just how wickedly selfish and greedy your fraudulent activities were," Judge Treviño said.

"You used the Johnston family's hard-earned money to pursue other business ventures that had the potential to reap you even greater financial rewards at their expense."

Victim-blaming 'despicable'

Lawson pleaded guilty to seven counts of fraud, each related to different businesses set up for the Johnstons' banana and cattle farms, and associated farming services.

She committed the fraud as the Johnstons dealt with cyclones and floods, and an outbreak of Panama disease in 2020 that temporarily forced them to stop producing bananas.

The court heard Lawson used money from the fraud to buy and renovate a Tully clothing shop. (Supplied)

Judge Treviño said Lawson co-operated with authorities "once the game was up" but she did so "in the face of what was an overwhelming case".

However, he said he did not consider Lawson's guilty plea to be indicative of remorse, a view he said her psychological report backed up.

"What stands out when reading it, are your despicable attempts to lay blame for your fraudulent conduct at the feet of your victims," Judge Treviño said.

"Without insight into your offending, you risk repeating your behaviours should you ever find yourself in a similar position of trust in the future.

"There is no evidence you have ever attempted to apologise directly to [the Johnston family].

"That was, of course, always an option open to you."

Michelle Kathleen Lawson, 53, pleaded guilty to seven counts of fraud that took place over a six-year period in Tully. (Supplied)

On Friday, the court heard victim impact statements from members of the Johnston family, who outlined how the emotional toll and financial consequences of Lawson's crimes would live with them for generations to come.

The fraud cost them opportunities to buy neighbouring farmland and hire more staff, the court heard.

"To learn that someone I had trusted and helped for so long had been deceiving us every day and continuing to smile at us, was almost impossible to accept," 81-year-old family matriarch Jill Johnston said.

The Johnstons managed to recover almost $1.5 million through civil action but the legal fees and related expenses cost them $500,000, on top of an emotional toll, the court heard.

Michelle Kathleen Lawson, 53, worked in the Far North Queensland town of Tully. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Mrs Johnston's daughter Melanie told the court she had to give up secure employment interstate to return to Tully to assist with the case.

The Johnston family and their supporters filled the courtroom gallery in Cairns for Lawson's plea and sentencing hearings, while Lawson appeared by video link from a Townsville prison.

She nodded as Judge Treviño handed down his sentence.

Lawson will be eligible for parole in August 2028.

title: Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
text:
Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.

With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.

Marnus Labuschagne picked a good time to score a century ahead of the first Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).

Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.

Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.

Darren Lehmann sees clear reasons for the decline in Test batting, with serious consequences for the game (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.

The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.

ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.

Steve Smith, Travis Head and Alex Carey have all averaged more than 40 over the past 18 Tests. Marnus Labuschagne is in the 20s. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.

We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.

To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.

Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.

It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.

The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.

This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.

Ricky Ponting was at his peak in the early 2000s. (ABC News)

The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.

To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.

The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.

Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.

But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.

Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.

In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.

From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.

It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.

The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.

In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.

The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.

Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.

The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.

The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.

But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26

That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.

To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.

So, why is this happening?

Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.

Darren Lehmann (right) as coach of Australia in 2014, with the current head of selectors, George Bailey, and the late Rod Marsh. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.

"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.

"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"

"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."

The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.

"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.

Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.

"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.

The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.

"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.

"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."

Mitchell Starc can be relied on to take wickets. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."

Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.

Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.

Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.

"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."

Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.

title: News anchor Richard Morecroft remembered as a 'great Australian'
text:
Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft is being remembered as a consummate professional and "a great Australian".

The 70-year-old died "at a time of his choosing", a statement on Instagram said, after he received a cancer diagnosis earlier this year.

"We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," the statement said.

Morecroft graced television screens for decades as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor for almost 20 years, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS.

Doogue (left) and Morecroft presenting the news together. (Supplied: Instagram)

Geraldine Doogue worked with Morecroft as co-host on The National in 1985, when her late husband Ian Carroll changed the half-hour 7PM television bulletin to an hour-long news and current affairs program.

Doogue told 702 ABC Sydney that she was shocked by his death and said his professionalism was a big part of his legacy.

"He was just terribly good to me and to my late husband ... during that really tumultuous year," she said.

"I mean, he was very much for it. Richard, once he was in, he was in. He was a very loyal, he contributed massively."

Veteran news anchor and television presenter, Richard Morecroft, is being remembered in tributes. (Supplied: Instagram)

Doogue said he had a strong sense of what "an ABC authority ought to be" and modelled it "effortlessly".

"He had quite a wit about him, but he fundamentally felt his role, I think, was to be that face of the ABC while he was doing this," she said.

" He looked out for people who weren't born and bred to that particular spot, which is very admirable, I think. "

Loading...

He also hosted wildlife and educational programs and wrote about nature and the environment.

Morecroft eventually moved to the NSW south coast, which Doogue said he called "his cathedral", with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay.

"He had this whole side in him that was artistic, very much involved with the natural world," she said.

"He just thrived in that environment and gave enormously to [and was] very generous to all sorts of charities."

Fostering younger talent

Australian Story ABC presenter and friend, Leigh Sales, told ABC 702 Sydney Mornings she first saw Morecroft on TV while watching Behind the News at school in the 1980s.

Sales says Morecroft spoke with her just after she started working at the ABC.

Sales said when she moved from Brisbane to Sydney as a young reporter at 22, he checked in with her to see how she was settling in.

"And at that age, I was like, 'Oh my God, the newsreader's speaking to me'. But that's what he was like," she said.

Sales is often seen speaking with young journalists and producers, helping to foster the next generation.

"I try really hard to be a good listener and to not be just telling people, 'Well, here's how I do it'," she said.

"The other thing that I feel like I learned from him is it doesn't matter if you're the star, you muck in like one of the team and you're not better than anyone else."

Richard Morecroft at the 2025 Sculpture in the Valley festival with festival director Stuart McCreery. (ABC News: ABC Illawarra/Rory Macdonald)

'A twinkle in his eye'

Former ABC presenter Keith Conlon, who met Morecroft when they worked together at a student radio station in Adelaide in the 1970s, said his fellow broadcaster was always a "lovely, warm person".

"We kind of invented community radio on the run, and Richard was one of those people who came through the door — he was an arts student [at University of Adelaide]," he said.

"He wasn't one of those 'out there' types … Very articulate, very intelligent.

" You just knew you were dealing with a person of substance. "

Conlon said originally, Morecroft expressed interest in potentially becoming a teacher or an actor, but that it made sense he turned to news reading.

"If you're a newsreader, you are in a way acting. You only run the gamut from A to B but you've got to try to lift that news off the page and give things a different nuance," he said.

Conlon said Morecroft had "a twinkle in his eye". (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Conlon said he was "delightful" with "a twinkle in his eye".

"He had a beautiful voice — just that lovely tone, but much more than that, he had a considered way of talking," he said.

"He loved the language, he loved the sense of what we were talking about, and he was dedicated to doing those things right. He was a perfectionist.

" But if you'd called him a star he would have cringed. "

'A figure of absolute trust'

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that Morecroft was a "great Australian".

"Combining a consummate professionalism with an unyielding humanity, Richard was a figure of absolute trust, a warm and familiar presence who guided us through the good times and bad," he said.

"He loved the arts and was deeply passionate about our natural environment.

"Nothing completed the picture so delightfully as the time we learned that he used to keep a baby flying fox safe and sound beneath the desk while he was presenting the news."

Tributes are flowing for veteran news anchor and television presenter, Richard Morecroft. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

702 ABC Sydney Mornings host Hamish Macdonald said he grew up watching Morecroft on the news.

"I think he's part of why I wanted to go into journalism. Really, he was just such a reliable, friendly, trusted voice," he said.

Nightlife host Philip Clark also recalled Morecroft as a "terrific fellow".

"Total professional as a newsreader and broadcaster as well," he said.

title: Landowner pushes back against opposition to Goolwa's first McDonald's
text:
The landowner where Goolwa's first McDonald's could be built has pushed back against local opposition, saying residents have a "democratic right" to choose what to eat or drink.

Mick McArdle's commercial property at Hutchinson Street is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to approval of a development application expected to be lodged with the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon.

But it has faced vocal opposition, first from a volunteer group dedicated to protecting Goolwa's culinary and cultural heritage, and then from Alexandrina Council, which recently voted to oppose establishing chain-based fast-food outlets in the seaside town.

The property is under contract and a development application is expected soon. (891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn)

"I don't think that people should have the right to take away other people's democratic right to choose what they eat or drink," Mr McArdle said.

"It's not just a one-way street.

"A lot of people actually like the idea of having a McDonald's here.

Alexandrina Council last month voted in favour of Cr Peter Oliver's motion, which stated that 38 food outlets in the area, including restaurants, cafes, supermarkets and service stations, already offer food.

The motion passed, but not unanimously.

It followed lobbying by Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group of about 250 members.

Goolwa was the first Australian town to be accredited by Cittaslow International in 2007, a European movement that promotes quality of life and sustainability in towns and cities, and handed a "slow town" status.

Cittaslow Goolwa vice-president Christine Putland said recently that the town already sold takeaway hamburgers and did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more.

"Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," she said in August.

A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa from Italy in 2007 to present the council with a certificate. (Website: Cittaslow Goolwa)

But Mr McArdle, who has lived in the town since 1978 and runs an automotive repair business on the site, said a significant portion of the town's population of more than 8,000 wanted a McDonald's because it would give young people work, and create more competition for takeaway food.

"Competition has to be good for the people in Goolwa; competition keeps the prices at a reasonable level," Mr McArdle said.

"And one of the service stations where you come into town has golden fried chicken, pizzas, the whole lot.

" It's all fast food, so why do you discriminate against one fast food and not another? "

He acknowledged he had a vested interest in the situation, but pointed out members of Cittaslow Goolwa involved with food outlets did as well.

"At the end of the day, if the development application ticks all the boxes as far as zoning and all that sort of stuff, then why should they [McDonald's] not be able to go in there?" Mr McArdle said.

Residents fight McDonald's Advocates for Goolwa's heritage attractions say the site of a former automotive repair business has been targeted for a McDonald's.

Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said there were "definitely people in the town" who backed a McDonald's but "the vast majority didn't".

"It would be interesting to know whether the people that are in favour are long-term residents or fairly new residents to the area," he said.

He agreed that a McDonald's would require local staff.

"However, the small businesses in the town at the moment and around the place, struggle to get staff as it is, particularly in the hospitality area," Mr Parkes said.

"It's very seasonal down here."

Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula, which is located 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor.

"It will be very interesting, when eventually all the information comes out in the open, just where we stand with who's for and who's against it, and their reasons," Mr Parkes said.

He reiterated that any development application requiring a change of use for the site would not go to the council for consideration.

It would go to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel — an independent body established under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016.

title: ‘It’ll hurt cricket’: CA boss’ warning to curators amid two-day Test fears
text:

SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘It’ll hurt cricket’: CA boss’ warning to curators amid two-day Test fears Daniel Brettig October 7, 2026 — 4:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Durban: Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg has revealed he told curators at major venues to prepare flatter pitches for this summer and beyond, amid fears about a recent spate of two-day Test matches that have damaged the game’s finances. Greenberg’s presence at the annual conclave of groundsmen was unusual by his own admission, but underlined the rising level of concern about matches being played “in fast forward” on grassy pitches with a souped-up Kookaburra ball. The Boxing Day Ashes Test was over in two days. Chris Hopkins Three of Australia’s past seven Tests have ended in two days, including the Perth and Melbourne Ashes matches, which were estimated to have cost around $15 million in lost revenue. “I addressed the curators’ conference, not something I thought I’d do,” Greenberg said in Durban. “When I arrived, curators have been meeting apparently every year for a number of decades, and it’s been a while since they’ve seen the CEO come and talk. So I think that maybe sent a message.

Advertisement

“What we’ve said is if you’re erring on which side of the line to roll on, then make it flatter, maybe slightly less grass, because the game has evolved over time. The way batters are batting and players are playing cricket. I’m not sure if our wickets have kept pace with that. The data and the stats certainly tell you that. “I am worried about short Test matches over time. I think a one-off is fine. You can deal with it. But over time, if we continue to see that trend, that will hurt the sport. It’ll hurt cricket, both from a commercial lens, but also just the purity of Test cricket and the beauty of a five-day close draw is as much a part of the fabric of Test cricket than a win or a loss, and so I don’t think we want to lose that.” Loading Greenberg has previously stated that the MCG and SCG Tests would not be moving in the event of BBL clubs being sold to private investors who may want a clear window for the tournament. But he has now conceded there is nothing guaranteed after the expiry of government and broadcast deals in 2032. “So we’ve said in the way we’ve pitched our documents and the way the process would work is the Sydney Test match is contracted right through until 2032, so it’s contracted both with government and it’s also contracted in our broadcast negotiations,” he said. “What happens beyond 2032, I think, is a question that we will have to address.

Whatever the success or failure of the pre-COP meeting in Fiji, it is clear the Albanese government will wear a political cost for putting it on. Normally, these annual gatherings are small affairs attended only by officials whose job it is to narrow the scope of climate negotiations at the sprawling UN Paris Treaty negotiations to follow. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, left, with former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern in Nadi, Fiji, on Wednesday. Getty Images But after Australia lost the bid to host the next COP to Turkey, the price Climate Minister Chris Bowen extracted for conceding was his role as president of negotiations, and the agreement that a leaders’ level pre-COP would be held in the Pacific. This way Australia could rattle the can for donations to the region from far-flung nations for the eye-bleeding cost of climate mitigation in the Pacific, elevate its climate concerns, and show off the damage already done to low-lying nations to demonstrate the immediate threat of climate change.

The problem is that few of those leaders made the trip. Indeed, just two from outside the Pacific fronted – those of Timor-Leste and Mauritius. Loading Having talked up the event, this leaves Albanese and Bowen in the awkward position of having to justify the $20 million-plus cost of hosting a party where the glamour guests did not turn up. With a budget in deficit and interest rates climbing, Australian voters are getting twitchy with the government spending their tax money on their own needs, let alone those of their regional neighbours. Little surprise that opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan labelled the event a farce.

Despite the disappointment at the roll-call, the mood on the ground was more positive. “In all my conversations, with the prime minister of Tuvalu yesterday, the minister from Tuvalu, the Secretary General of PIF, they couldn’t be happier with the focus we brought to the Pacific.” Albanese speaking at one of the final pre-COP31 events. title: Home construction is up but still well short of government targets
text:
Advertisement

A surge in homes built last quarter has failed to get the government back on track for its 1.2 million homes target, as experts warn the deteriorating economic conditions threaten to slow down future housing projects. The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its quarterly building activity data on Wednesday, showing a boost to the number of homes that began construction and the number of projects finished in the June quarter. But it also showed Labor remained almost 100,000 short of the homes needed to reach its target of building a record number of dwellings over five years – a key plank in its plan to tackle the housing crisis and get more first home buyers into the market. Housing commencements and completions surged in the last quarter. Sitthixay Ditthavong The number of homes, including houses and apartments, that began construction in the June quarter rose 7 per cent, to 52,201. Homes that were completed rose 5.8 per cent to 47,168. But the home building sector has this year been hit by a series of interest rate hikes, higher construction prices due to the Middle East war and uncertainty prompted by the May budget’s housing tax changes which are yet to properly flow through to the figures.

Advertisement

KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said the uptick in commencements and completions showed Australia was trending in the right direction, and a record number of more than 240,000 houses under construction would enter the market over the next year or so. “Developers are seeing that prices are softening, their holding costs are increasing... so they’re probably on the bike pedaling as fast as they can to complete projects and get them into the market,” he said. But projects starting today would be more expensive because they break ground after the US’s war on Iran and the increased oil costs which flow on to construction, he said. “This is probably as good as it’s going to get for the foreseeable future,” he said.

Advertisement

Housing Industry Association chief economist Tim Reardon said the 52,000 commencements in the quarter would not be enough to keep up with demand. “There hasn’t been a material increase in the volume of new home building over the past decade, we’re still building a similar volume… despite the pickup that we can see in today’s data, it’s about average for recent decades,” he said. “We have not built enough homes in the past year to meet growth and demand, and we don’t anticipate that in the next 12 months we’ll build enough homes to meet the growth in demand.” Reardon said the number of houses would likely continue to rise in the September quarter because of the strength of the market coming into 2026, but they could start to fall by early 2027.

Advertisement

Related Article Property prices It will take a generation to fix the housing crisis, says top economist “What today’s data shows us is just how much momentum there was in the housing market coming into this year,” he said. “That growth isn’t going to be sustained, and that we won’t see an increase in home building activity in 2027.” The association estimates the failure to hit the government’s housing targets has left an $11 billion “black hole” in the finances of state and territory governments because not enough stamp duty and GST was collected over the two years since the target was set. Had the target been on track, the construction would have generated $45 billion in economic activity and potentially housed 242,160 Australians based on average household sizes, the housing association said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said there was still more work to do on housing construction. Louie Douvis

Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Housing Minister Clare O’Neil released a statement on Wednesday welcoming the June quarter increase in dwelling commencements and completions. “These are encouraging numbers, but we know they can bounce around from quarter to quarter and that there’s more work to do,” it said. “We are tackling housing supply from all angles, including funding enabling infrastructure, building 55,000 social and affordable homes and working with states and territories to streamline approvals.” But Master Builders Australia chief executive Denita Wawn said the outlook for new projects was increasingly challenging. “The cumulative impact of the federal budget, continued interest rate increases and an ongoing global uncertainty have deteriorated the environment.”

title: ‘A mystery’: The men fuelling Victoria’s record drug overdose toll
