Fatal overdoses among Gen X men have increased by almost 50 cent in Victoria in a single year, driving the state’s drug-related deaths to their highest levels since the heroin glut of the late 1990s. A new Coroner’s Court report shows 632 overdose fatalities were recorded in Victoria last year – the highest number since the court began collecting data in 2000. New Coroner’s Court data shows a marked increase in overdose deaths among men aged 45–54. Istock Men aged 45 to 54 were more likely to die from a drug overdose than any other age group, with the number of deaths in this cohort rising from 106 in 2024 to 156 last year – a rise of 47 per cent. The report said it was not known what was driving the rise among this age group.

Advertisement

“An increase of 50 [fatal overdoses] in a single cohort in one year has not been observed in any other group for the reporting period,” the report said. John Ryan, chief executive of public health research and drug policy organisation the Penington Institute, said the unprecedented rise in deaths among Gen X men was “a bit of a mystery” that needed further investigation. Ryan said he suspected that GPs becoming more cautious about prescribing addictive drugs, as well as real-time prescription monitoring, had led to middle-aged men previously addicted to pharmaceutical drugs being pushed into Victoria’s illicit drug market. “There’s a possibility that people have shifted from pharmaceutical misuse to illicit drug use. This is much more risky because they don’t know the quality or quantity of what they’re consuming,” he said.

Advertisement

“There hasn’t been enough support for off-ramping people out of pharmaceutical drugs.” Ryan said a shortage of Victorian GPs who prescribe medication to treat addiction also made it difficult for users to access treatment such as methadone. “This is a story of great tragedy,” he said. “It’s not just about the people who are lost, it’s about the people who are left behind to suffer.” The top contributing drugs to the fatal overdoses were heroin (261 deaths), methamphetamine (249 deaths) and the prescription medication diazepam, widely known by the brand name Valium (232 deaths). Many deaths involved multiple drugs. Three-quarters of overdose deaths over the past decade were unintentional, while about 19 per cent were suicides, and 6 per cent of cases were unknown. Men were on average twice as likely as women to die from overdose.

Advertisement

The Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association described the situation as a public health crisis and called for greater investment in harm reduction initiatives. Related Article Healthcare ‘A slow-moving train wreck’: Victoria’s drug treatment system in crisis “The fact that the annual overdose deaths have now surpassed 600 should be an immediate call to action,” said the organisation’s interim chief executive, Scott Drummond. “This is more than double Victoria’s road toll. There are more and more families impacted by this.” There is record demand for alcohol and drug treatment services in Victoria, with more than 5122 people currently on waiting lists, according to a recent survey from the association.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The overdose death rate of 8.9 deaths per 100,000 people in Victoria remained relatively stable over the past decade. Though this was an increase from 8.5 deaths in 2024, the coroner’s report found the increase over time was related to the state’s population growth. State Coroner Judge Liberty Sanger said the “deeply concerning” deaths highlighted the need for a strong public health response. “Drug-related harms are complex and affect communities all across Victoria – it is vital that vulnerable people can access appropriate supports, treatment and education,” Sanger said. Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said the government acknowledged there was more to do. “Every overdose death is a preventable tragedy – and I extend my sympathies to the friends and families impacted by the loss of a loved one to overdose,” Stitt said.

It splurged $65,000 on a recruiter, then chose an existing employee “Whether it’s introducing pill testing, installing naloxone dispensing machines, or expanding access to rehabilitation beds across the state, we’re getting on with the job of addressing and reducing drug harms in our community.” The minister said the government would continue to roll out its $95 million statewide action plan that aims to increase access to opioid pharmacotherapy across community health services, target health and social supports, and introduce the state’s first alcohol and drug-related strategy – a 10-year plan for a holistic approach to reduce alcohol and other drug-related harm and stigma. Stitt also said Labor had doubled the number of residential rehabilitation beds since coming to government in 2014, with a focus on regional and rural areas. “The majority of these increases have been in rural and regional Victoria with brand-new facilities delivered for Corio, Wangaratta, and Traralgon – collectively providing care and support to an additional 900 Victorians a year. title: ‘Groundbreaking’: High Court quashes coal mine expansion over climate emissions
text:
Advertisement

Approval for a major coal mine expansion has been declared invalid by the High Court in a decision that will force NSW planning authorities to reckon with emissions from Australian coal burnt overseas. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government was still considering the 111-page judgment handed down on Wednesday, while casting doubt on whether the decision would set a national precedent. Heavy machinery working at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant Coal Mine Operations near Muswellbrook. Kate Geraghty But the federal opposition is demanding the Albanese government intervene should the NSW Labor government fail to urgently pass new laws. One Nation deputy leader Barnaby Joyce echoed the call for new legislation, arguing that the court decision would make Australia poorer. “Poorer nations cannot pay for the public infrastructure and the social security benefits that are part of the birthright of this nation,” Joyce said. The NSW government has been contacted for comment.

Advertisement

Anita Hart, a lawyer for the local environment group fighting the project, celebrated the victory, calling it “a groundbreaking decision for climate law in Australia” that would be studied closely by other countries. Related Article Mining Courts turn on coal mines over climate impacts The Greens’ new deputy federal leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it would send a clear message to both government and business that “when Australian coal is burnt overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port”. The case revolved around an open-cut coal mine at Mount Pleasant in the NSW Hunter region, a political battleground eyed by both the Coalition and One Nation. Owner MACH Energy Australia won approval in 2022 to significantly expand the mine and extend its life by 22 years. It outlined measures to address domestic greenhouse gas emissions from the project.

Advertisement

But it also concluded that 98 per cent of the total emissions would be classed as “scope 3”, a category for further use of a product, such as the burning of coal for energy after export. The owner argued these emissions would be managed “in accordance with customer countries commitments under the Paris Agreement” and would not “contribute to Australian greenhouse gas emissions”. Neither the NSW Department Planning and Environment nor the ultimate decision maker, the Independent Planning Commission, took issue with the company’s position. The mine owner survived one legal challenge from environmentalists known as Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group Inc, before the tables then turned in the NSW Court of Appeal. The High Court on Wednesday upheld the lower court’s decision, but on a different basis.

Advertisement

Under NSW law, the Independent Planning Commission needed to consider imposing conditions on an approval to ensure “that greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable”. Justice James Edelman said: “Members of the Commission did not address that requirement with respect to scope 3 emissions, amounting to 98 per cent of the project’s emissions, because they considered that those emissions would be accounted for in the countries to which the coal was exported.” Edelman continued that “by focusing only upon two per cent of the project’s emissions”, the commission had failed to in its duty to fully consider minimisation conditions. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government was still working out the impacts of the decision. Alex Ellinghausen Justice Michelle Gordon said it was not the High Court’s role to weigh in on the merits of this requirement or to say what conditions might be imposed to minimise emissions. But Gordon found the failure to at least consider conditions was a “material” error that invalidated the expansion approval. Justice Robert Beech-Jones agreed.

Advertisement

Two other judges, Chief Justice Stephen Gageler and Justice Jayne Jagot, disagreed with the majority in finding that the planning commission had adequately considered emissions overseas. They quoted the commission’s finding that “with the adoption of the Paris Agreement, almost all countries have committed to reduce global [greenhouse gas] emissions and to track their progress in doing so”. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government had not had an opportunity to read the judgment in full, but its early assessment was the impact would be limited to NSW. “It doesn’t automatically transfer to Commonwealth decisions or Commonwealth legislation,” Watt told News24 shortly after the decision was handed down. Watt reiterated that scope 3 emissions did not need to be considered under federal law, but said other states may be impacted depending on their legislative settings.

Advertisement

In a joint statement released on Wednesday afternoon, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Nationals leader Matt Canavan described the decision as “absurd”, seeking to blame Labor for the ruling. “The decision turns on the wording of NSW planning law. That means it can be fixed, and fixed quickly. The Coalition calls on the Minns government to act immediately to introduce legislation amending the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act. “It must make clear that overseas emissions from Australia’s exported resources are not a consideration in project approvals,” the Coalition leaders said. “If the NSW state government won’t act, the Albanese Labor government should legislate to fix this issue and provide certainty to workers, business and our international energy partners.”

title: Mary Fowler’s latest decision tells us something we should already know about her
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportSoccerMatildas Mary Fowler’s latest decision tells us something we should already know about her Vince Rugari October 7, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When someone shows you who they are, as American writer and civil rights activist Maya Angelou once said, you should believe them the first time. Mary Fowler has shown us who she is. She is not exactly hiding it. She has told us, explicitly and proudly, about what makes her tick, the things that she truly values in life, and where soccer sits in her personal pecking order – and we admire her for this. But we don’t seem to be listening. Loading We are patiently waiting for her to finally find that permanent role in the Matildas’ starting XI so that we can watch her settle in and play there for the next decade. We dream of seeing her become an undisputed global superstar, winning Ballons d’Or and UEFA Champions League medals, leading the Matildas and Australian soccer towards greatness, all without wondering if she actually wants any of these things, or if we just want them for us, via her. Fowler is reportedly back in Sydney visiting her partner, Penrith Panthers NRL star Nathan Cleary, as he recovers from a career-threatening broken leg. These are presumably the unexplained “personal circumstances” that led to her pulling out of the Matildas’ friendlies against Germany and Haiti – but since nothing has been said officially, we still don’t know for sure.

Advertisement

Regardless, coach Joe Montemurro has been denied a critical opportunity to advance his preparations for next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup, insofar as where Fowler fits into those plans. These are not “only friendlies”; this team will have just a handful of games together before the tournament begins, and Fowler has rarely been fully fit since Montemurro began in the job in June 2025. She is such a special player, Australia’s World Cup hopes rest at least partly on her shoulders. It exposes a tension between the inherent collective demands of international soccer and individual autonomy to decide what matters most in a player’s life. Mary Fowler and Nathan Cleary. Instagram In Fowler’s case, it forces us to confront the possibility that her idea of her career might look very different to ours. “Obviously I enjoy playing football, but I wouldn’t say it’s my passion,” Fowler said last year on the Keegan and Company podcast, recorded in the days after she underwent surgery on her ACL.

Advertisement

When she was much younger, soccer was her “everything”, she explained. These days, it’s just her job. That doesn’t mean she’s not committed – obviously, she is – but it helps us understand her perspective. “I play it because there are a lot of things I enjoy about it,” she said. “I really enjoy travelling, being with my teammates, the people that I’ve met through football, but if I finished it tomorrow, I probably wouldn’t have any regrets. There’s other things outside of football I am more passionate about.” Mary Fowler on the ball for the Matildas in June. Getty Images It would be totally understandable, then, for Fowler to want to be by Cleary’s side at a time of serious trauma, and for that to outweigh her desire to play. If Fowler or Football Australia had confirmed this was why she wasn’t available for the Matildas, many people would have congratulated her for setting boundaries. She went even deeper on these topics in her book, Bloom, released last year, in which she detailed her thought process during the last time she withdrew from a Matildas camp, in late 2024. She publicly cited “physical and mental fatigue” – and she was applauded for her bravery – but when she first approached the team to ask for some time off, “the response wasn’t as supportive as I’d hoped,” she wrote.

Advertisement

Fowler was told it would not be a good look, that the Matildas risked the appearance of “favouritism” and that it could open a “can of worms” within the squad. “Although I noted the amount of pressure being put on me to still come in, I’m glad I stood firm in my decision,” she wrote. Mary Fowler is only 23, but has a maturity well beyond her age. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I made it known that, with all due respect, I was going to do what was best for me. There was a lot that didn’t sit well with me in the way those discussions were handled, but eventually I was given approval to pull out of the camp. I didn’t enjoy feeling like I was a commodity, but I understood that sometimes that’s just the ruthless side of business … no matter what pressures or backlash you face, you shouldn’t feel guilty for making yourself a priority.” Fowler is still only 23, but has a maturity well beyond her age. This is someone who meditates, who journals, who has thought all of this through, football and life, at a deeper level, and determined that the former is just a small part of the latter.

Advertisement

Honestly, good for her. Many people go through their entire lives without figuring this stuff out. But multiple things can be true at once: that Fowler is entitled to make the call she believes is right for herself, and that others, including her teammates, coaches and Matildas supporters, don’t have to love it. This is, as she put it, the ruthless side of the business. The Australian jersey is not a mere work uniform, but a representation of something much larger than the person wearing it: of fans who have emotionally invested in this team precisely for these reasons; of players and staff who accept that pursuing a common goal sometimes requires putting the collective above themselves; of every other aspiring footballer who would drop everything for the chance to pull it on, even just once. There is a reason it is referred to as “international duty.” It is a duty. When you have been selected to play for your country, availability is supposed to be the default position.

Advertisement

Of course, soccer does not come before everything, and there are times when players are given leave on compassionate grounds. Related Article Updated

Friendlies ‘I only just found out’: Fowler’s Matildas teammates in the dark over sudden withdrawal But there are also times when players would rather be somewhere else for perfectly compelling personal reasons and turn up anyway, because representing your country demands a higher level of sacrifice. They routinely leave partners and children behind, surrender precious time at home, travel enormous distances, which put strain on their bodies and minds, and sometimes face pressure from the clubs who actually pay their day-to-day wages. Opinions will vary as to whether returning home to comfort an injured partner reaches this undefined threshold. Fowler is absolutely entitled to decide that soccer isn’t the most important thing in her life, but when it comes to choosing not to play for the Matildas, there could also be footballing consequences.

Advertisement

What could those consequences be? That’s a thorny question, and one for Montemurro and Football Australia to tackle as they see fit, depending on their discussions with Fowler, the feelings of the rest of the squad and balancing those against her status as a generational talent. Based on what she has told us about herself, Fowler may well accept any consequences as the price of her own peace of mind. And the rest of us should probably accept that, too. We can continue dreaming of everything Fowler might achieve in football, but we shouldn’t assume she shares all of those dreams with us.

title: Frenchie
text:
The allure of Frenchie is multi-faceted, but the drawcard that really matters is simple: value. Yes, the room is moody and vibey, and the menu is full of dishes that capture some of the current edible zeitgeist – a little bit French, a touch playful, mostly snacky. But the point of difference here is that everything costs $14.

Everything? Well, yes, practically everything. You can buy a bottle rather than one of the ($14) glasses of wine, and they serve basic soft drinks for less. You can add fries to certain dishes for an extra $7. But everything else – the cocktails, the caviar bumps, the oysters (three per serve), the steak – is $14.

Silky beetroot-cured salmon gravlax rests on foamy green sorrel sauce. Grilled duck breast comes drizzled with a l’orange sauce. Eggplant is cooked to a pleasing slump and smothered in a goat’s cheese sauce. Dishes may not blow your mind, but most are perfectly acceptable.

As for the vibe? The collective relief of a room full of people who know they can have this much fun, without worrying too much about the damage when the bill comes, is downright exhilarating.

Must order: A martini (or three), made with a touch of absinthe, served in a beautiful coupe.

Cumulus Inc. was one of the city’s first wine-bar-slash-restaurants, and an early pioneer of the familiar-but-fun dinner menu served in a stylish industrial space.

Head chef Hannah Holleran’s menu may not look particularly inventive or singular – then the food hits the table. There are dozens of tuna tartares in this city, but very few are this fresh, served in hefty cubes over goat’s curd and vibrant green peas spiked with mint. Tender agnolotti, filled with beetroot ricotta and garnished with walnuts and sage, makes for an excellent mid-course before a 1.3-kilogram lamb shoulder arrives, fall-apart tender and smothered in an almond and red pepper sauce.

Cumulus Inc. is not only the model from which some of Melbourne’s best restaurants took inspiration, it continues to shine brightly as a standard-bearer of great service, fantastic wine and approachable, exciting and delicious dining.

This swanky steakhouse no longer holds the crown for Melbourne’s go-to special occasion restaurant, but fewer venues in town boast such a massive menu, and such wide appeal.

If you’re here for luxury ingredients done right, you will almost certainly be happy. The quality of the product is undeniable, from ultra-fresh Merimbula oysters to whole grilled Hervey Bay prawns, fat and juicy and flavoured with curry leaves and Kampot pepper.

And what about the steaks? The menu offers a wide choice of cuts, charred over a wood grill and cooked to exactly the right temperature, every time.

Does Rockpool still have a place in our dining landscape? Almost certainly. For the business lunch, absolutely. To just have a reliably good steak and martini and not have to think too much? Well, there are certainly other options these days, but this isn’t a bad one, not by a mile.

Platina Resources has fired up the drill rig for a second time, kicking off an aircore drilling campaign at its Granite Well East prospect, which forms part of the company’s Mt McKenna gold project just 13 kilometres east of Laverton in Western Australia. The 53-hole, 3200-metre program is designed to follow up highly encouraging gold mineralisation hits from a previous campaign and will test strike continuity and the system’s lateral extent. Drilling rig at Platina Resources Mt McKenna gold project near Laverton in Western Australia. The new work at Granite Well East follows an earlier phase-three program that unearthed multiple mineralised zones, including a notable one-metre hit of a hefty 7.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 40m. Several intercepts from that campaign either finished in mineralisation or near the bottom of the hole, hinting the system remains open at depth. Other encouraging results from the earlier drilling included a 4-metre section grading 1.11g/t gold from just 12m, associated with a strong arsenic anomaly and a separate 7-metre intercept going 0.61g/t gold from 36m that continued to the bottom of the hole. A further hole delivered 4m grading 0.93g/t gold from 52m, also ending at the bottom of the hole.

‘This drill program is designed to test the potential strike continuity and lateral extent of the gold mineralisation.’ Platina Resources managing director Dr Paul Polito The company is well-funded for the push after banking the final US$2 million (A$2.9M) payment from the sale of its Owendale scandium project to mining goliath Rio Tinto. The deal, which closed in stages over three years, delivered a whopping US$14 million (AU$20M) into Platina’s coffers. Platina Resources managing director Dr Paul Polito said: “The results of the program will assist in determining the scale, continuity and significance of mineralisation and guide subsequent exploration, such as reverse circulation drilling or induced polarisation surveys.” The project’s address has a rich pedigree, sitting adjacent to Genesis Minerals’ 3.9-million-ounce Laverton project and just 20km north-east of Gold Fields’ 3.9-million-ounce Granny Smith gold mine. The Granite Well East target itself lies at what is interpreted to be the intersection of two major structural corridors, a setting often favourable for trapping gold-bearing fluids. Notably, the Laverton district remains a hive of exploration activity, with nearby explorers continuing to deliver positive news flow - a backdrop further enhanced by a robust Australian-dollar gold price, currently sitting around the A$6000-per-ounce mark.

The company’s savvy exploration model of advancing early-stage projects before monetising them to fund the next generation of opportunities looks to be paying dividends. The Owendale scandium sale to Rio proved a textbook example, shifting the capital and development risk of a specialist critical minerals project to a major with the balance sheet to handle it, while leaving Platina cashed-up to chase gold. The company has also demonstrated its willingness to take the tin-snips to its portfolio, having previously sold its Xanadu project, relinquished Challa and farmed out Brimstone to other explorers. Beyond Mt McKenna, Platina still holds its Sunrise Bore project, 44km south of Laverton, which previously delivered a solid 29m at 3.38g/t gold from just 11m. That hit included an 11-metre core grading an eye-catching 8.62g/t alongside further intersections of 18m at 1.12g/t and 37m running 0.43g/t. The first campaign tested just 200m of a much bigger 1.2km mineralised trend sitting within a broader 3.6km structural corridor, leaving plenty of untouched ground for the drill bit to chew through. Platina’s portfolio also includes the earlier-stage Mt Morgans South prospect, 35km south-west of Laverton. The 126.4-square-kilometre patch of ground sits near Genesis Minerals’ three-million-tonne-per-annum Mt Morgans processing plant and its 1.4 million-ounce Westralia gold deposit, highlighting the strategic nature of the address. With the Rio Tinto deal now financially complete, a healthy bank balance, and the drill rods turning in one of WA’s most productive and richly endowed gold districts, Platina’s focus now appears to be shifting squarely to unearthing a meaningful discovery. Pornhub is switching explicit content back on for Australian iPhone and iPad users who have confirmed their age with Apple, seven months after its owner gutted the site in protest at the new age verification laws. Aylo, the Montreal-based company behind Pornhub, said on Wednesday that age-verified iOS users in Australia would now be served “a standard adult user experience”. The statement made no change for Android or desktop users. Pornhub’s Canadian parent company previously cut off Australian users rather than comply with age check laws. Getty Since March 9, when the eSafety Commissioner’s Age-Restricted Material Codes took effect, Aylo has served Australian visitors a stripped-back version of Pornhub. Explicit videos were replaced with podcasts, lifestyle segments and branded merchandise, as this masthead reported at the time. The codes require high-risk services such as Pornhub to check users are over 18 before showing them pornography. Breaches carry penalties of up to $49.5 million each.

Advertisement

Aylo’s reversal is largely on the back of updates to Apple’s settings. Since September, Australians have had to confirm they are adults, by scanning an identity document or using a credit card, before downloading 18+ apps or switching off certain safety settings. Apple’s web content filter and communication safety tools are switched on automatically for anyone who has not confirmed they are over 18. Scarlet Alliance chief executive Mish Pony and president Jenna Love. Simon Schluter “In our view, Apple’s Australian device-level age-verification update offers one of the strongest and hardest to circumvent protections currently available for helping prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content,” Aylo said in a statement from Alex Kekesi, its vice-president of brand and community. Aylo has argued for years that age checks belong on the device rather than on individual websites. It said this approach protected children “without requiring adults to surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites”, and avoided systems that could be dodged with a VPN.

Related Article Harassment The day porn turned off: Inside Australia’s high-stakes war with the adult industry Aylo did not say how Pornhub identifies which visitors have passed Apple’s check, or whether eSafety had approved the approach. Sex workers had warned the restrictions would cost them money. Scarlet Alliance, the national peak body for sex workers, told this masthead in March that blocking compliant sites would push viewers to offshore platforms that are less likely to check who appears in their videos or to take down content uploaded without consent. “That leaves sex workers not earning income from their content,” Mish Pony, the group’s chief executive, said at time, “with obvious flow-on effects – lower earnings and being pushed into working in ways that are less safe.” Wednesday’s change restores full access only for iPhone and iPad users who have confirmed their age with Apple.

Advertisement

The regulator stopped short of endorsing the move. An eSafety spokesperson said services could use a range of age-assurance methods as long as they could show those methods were “fair, accurate, robust and effective” and complied with Australian privacy law. “It remains the responsibility of individual services, including Aylo, the provider of Pornhub, to ensure the measures they use meet their obligations under the Online Safety Act,” the spokesperson said. eSafety encouraged a “layered approach” to age assurance. Aylo has fought age verification laws across several markets. It claimed Pornhub’s traffic fell 77 per cent in Britain after similar rules came in there, before it blocked UK visitors entirely. In March, two VPN apps jumped more than 100 places in Australian App Store rankings within hours of the codes taking effect. eSafety designed its codes to work across several layers of the internet. If a non-compliant site keeps serving children, the regulator can lean on Apple and Google through the App Store code to block it. Aylo is now urging Google and Microsoft to copy Apple’s approach and called on Apple to roll it out globally.“The technology exists. A precedent exists,” the company said. She owned a lovely house when we met, but sold it and lived off the proceeds, which has now all been spent. She now lives with her adult son, and has been in and out of casual work for years. On the other hand, I have another friend with a sick husband and three kids, and I’ve offered to loan her money anytime. She’s always declined. Stretching the friendship Mixing money with friendship carries a high risk of strain, awkwardness and resentment if repayment fails. Ask Financial expert Melissa Browne, who agreed to loan almost $300,000 to a friend on the proviso that it was for six weeks. The money was intended as a bridging loan for a business. title: My grandfather built Myer from nothing. The bile of this debate harms all of us
text:

NationalImmigration nation Opinion My grandfather built Myer from nothing. The bile of this debate harms all of us Michael Myer Contributor October 7, 2026 — 3:00pm

October 7, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A little over 125 years ago my grandfather, Sidney Myer, landed in Port Melbourne, penniless and with little English. Escaping the pogroms in tsarist Russia, he came in the hope that this country would offer him the safety, freedom and opportunity to begin a new life. Typical of so many immigrants before him and since, he started out with nothing, carting a haberdasher’s trading box on his back and selling door to door until he was able to open his first store in Bendigo in 1900. From there, he built the largest department store chain in the southern hemisphere by the time he died in 1934. The original Myer shop in Bendigo in 1905. Sidney Myer is pictured third from left. As the grandson of one of Australia’s most famous and most successful immigrants, it feels like my duty to make an intervention into the debate around the significance of immigration in the cultural, social and economic fabric of this country. As we watch the rise of populism in this country in the form of the One Nation Party, and its leader, Pauline Hanson, what seems to be lost is the profound contribution that immigrants have made, and will continue to make, to the strength and vibrancy of our nation if they are given the chance.

Advertisement

Sidney Myer’s deep commitment to this land that gave him a new home inspired him to build tirelessly and never stop giving back to those in need. This is best exemplified by the work he did funding the construction of Yarra Boulevard that kept hundreds of men employed during the Great Depression, and a massive Christmas dinner he held for the unemployed at the Melbourne Exhibition Centre in 1930 that drew more than 11,000 people across five separate sittings. Retailer and immigrant Sidney Myer. What drove him was the tireless entrepreneurial energy that also spurred so many of this country’s great entrepreneurial immigrants. Men such as Frank Lowy, Dick Pratt, Harry Triguboff and Maha Sinnathamby, who share that same energy. Together they helped shaped the culture, and the social and economic fabric of this country. Through their endeavours they have contributed hundreds of thousands of jobs, and their personal philanthropy has made further enduring impacts on the cultural and social landscape of our nation. What the increasingly strident populist voices being led by One Nation and its openly racist leader Pauline Hanson are doing is demonising, devaluing and degrading the timeless value that immigration and immigrants bring. Just some of the abhorrent comments she has made over the years include that we are “being swamped by Asians”, and that “Islam is a disease … we need to vaccinate ourselves against”. Now she wants to close the door to international students and to the families of skilled migrants.

Advertisement

The Coalition has followed, promising it would deliver “the biggest cut to immigration in the history of this country”. Related Article Opinion

Immigration nation I am the child of an immigrant. So are 51 per cent of Australians Eryk Bagshaw Investigative reporter In listening to these voices and giving comfort to anti-immigration rhetoric we are turning our backs on the enduring legacies of those great immigrants. In every facet of life – science, medicine, the arts, agriculture, industry, and politics – our lives are enriched by the energy, drive and inspiration immigrants bring to our collective lives. It is time for us to stop giving credence to voices that see immigrants as people taking from us and being a burden upon society, worthy of condemnation and censure. To demonise immigrants is essentially un-Australian. We all are enriched by our multicultural heritage and must resile from the notion of a “monocultural” Australia.

Advertisement

We cannot deny the fact that the tens of thousands who seek to build better lives in this country today, just as my grandfather did 125 years ago, do so with the energy, drive and determination to create new lives. They build businesses, drive innovation and contribute to the cultural, intellectual and social dynamism of this country. It’s undeniable that those who are prepared to take great risks in building anew can do great things. Denigrating immigration demeans the memory of all the immigrants who have gone before and blinds us to the contribution that today’s immigrants make now and will continue to make in the future. Let’s not allow a fear of foreigners to pollute our politics. We are all immigrants in this country. Michael Sidney Myer is the grandson of Sidney Myer. Forrestania Resources has quickly put its stamp on the recently acquired Tampia gold project in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region, tabling a maiden JORC-compliant mineral resource of 4.6 million tonnes grading 1.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 223,300 ounces of the precious metal. The estimate, which employed a 0.5g/t gold cut-off grade, marks a significant first step for Forrestania after acquiring the project from established gold producer Ramelius Resources in September. It immediately bolsters the company’s stated strategy of building a hub-and-spoke operation centred on its newly acquired Westonia Hub, which includes the Edna May gold processing facility. An aerial view of Forrestania Resources’ recently acquired Tampia open pit, previously mined by Ramelius Resources, 75 kilometres south of Merredin in Western Australia. The resource is split between an indicated 2.5 million tonnes at 1.47g/t gold for 118,500 ounces and 2.1 million tonnes at 1.56g/t gold for 104,800 ounces in the inferred category. The Tampia project is no stranger to production. Between 2021 and 2023, Ramelius mined an estimated 3 million tonnes from the open pit at a solid grade of 2.1g/t gold to produce around 201,100 ounces. That ore was trucked around 140 kilometres from Tampia to the very same Edna May plant that now sits in Forrestania’s stable.

Advertisement

‘Forrestania’s strategy of long-term gold production is supported by multiple deposits within haulage distance of infrastructure.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty The project is shaping up as a key plank in Forrestania’s ambitious two-hub production strategy. The company is building a classic hub-and-spoke gold machine, corralling satellite deposits around two processing workhorses – the 2.9-million-tonne-per-annum Edna May plant and the 3.2Mtpa Lake Johnston facility – with both earmarked to fire up in early 2027. Before Ramelius broke ground at Tampia, the project held a resource of 8.2 million tonnes at 1.7g/t gold for 460,000 ounces, highlighting the surprising scale of the original mineralised system. Forrestania’s maiden resource for Tampia effectively defines gold remaining beneath and around the existing open pit. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “This maiden estimate highlights a significant addition to the Forrestania Mineral Resources inventory, providing additional Mineral Resource ounces within trucking distance of the Edna May processing facility. With Tampia located within our newly acquired Westonia Hub, we believe this Mineral Resource will play an important role in Forrestania’s strategy of establishing long-term gold production.” The Tampia project is 75km south of Merredin. Geologically, it lies within the Lake Grace Terrane, part of the ancient almost three-billion-year-old Yilgarn Craton which dominates the southwestern quarter of WA.

Advertisement

Gold mineralisation is hosted in a mafic gneiss unit and occurs as shallow-dipping lode zones between 2m and 20m thick, which are considered amenable to conventional open-pit mining. In simple terms, mafic gneiss refers to a usually ancient, banded, coarse-grained metamorphic rock rich in dark, iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals. Forrestania’s mineralisation model was based on a massive historical drilling database of almost 4500 holes for more than 180,000m of drilling by a succession of owners including BHP, Explaurum and Ramelius. Critically, metallurgical testwork conducted by previous owner Explaurum suggests the ore is free-milling and delivers impressive recoveries. Oxide material demonstrated a gold recovery of more than 96 per cent, while fresh rock returned an average recovery of 91.4 per cent through a conventional carbon-in-leach circuit. The maiden resource at Tampia adds to Forrestania’s already significant two-million-ounce plus global inventory. The tally also includes a 285,700-ounce resource at its Lady Ada and Lady Magdalene deposits in the Forrestania Greenstone Belt, the northern tip of which lies an estimated 100km south of the WA town of Southern Cross. Those deposits have a history of high-grade, nuggety gold, with the old Blue Haze pit at Lady Ada previously producing 27,154 ounces at a stellar average grade of 8.81g/t gold.

title: 'I want to be here the rest of my life': Lionel Messi's emotional international retirement
text:
In brief Footballer Lionel Messi has played his final international match, scoring in a 3-0 win over Benin.

Messi announced he would retire from international matches following Argentina's World Cup final loss to Spain.

Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Wednesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savouring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as 'The Last Tango'.

"It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years," Messi told fans in a post-match address.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."

Messi, though, said he had no regrets about his decision to retire, citing Argentina's gruelling World Cup campaign, which took place as his late father was seriously ill, as a factor.

"Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through," said Messi.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina teammates made its way through crowds of well-wishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick-off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word "Gracias" (Thank You) above the football superstar's No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read "The Malvinas are Argentine", the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute — a tribute to Messi's famous shirt number — for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

'Gave it my all'

At the final whistle, a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi's image and thanking the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner for his career.

Messi's farewell came two and a half months after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote at the time.

Before Wednesday's game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

"To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!" he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed "The joy of my life."

Former Barcelona teammate and Brazil's all-time top goalscorer Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

"It's not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more," he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami in the US's Major League Soccer league until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi's departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country's 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona's heir.

"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

title: Think you can spot scam red flags? The warning signs are changing
text:
IN BRIEF ANZ has warned businesses about sophisticated scams in upcoming busy commerce periods.

Cybersecurity experts say AI improves every stage of a scam.

Australians are being warned that some of the most common advice for spotting scams is becoming less effective, as criminals use artificial intelligence to create convincing emails, phone calls and video deepfakes.

Banks and cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence (AI) is helping fraudsters impersonate trusted colleagues, businesses and even family members with a level of sophistication that can be almost impossible to detect.

The warning comes ahead of the Black Friday sales period and summer holidays, when scammers typically exploit heightened spending and pressure to target victims.

More than 84,000 cybercrime reports were made in 2025, while the average self-reported cost of cybercrime to businesses rose sharply, according to the Australian Signals Directorate.

How AI is changing the scam landscape

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

AI is transforming every stage of a scam, from impersonation to execution, according to Sanjay Jha, a professor at UNSW's School of Computer Science and Engineering.

"What’s genuinely new is three things: the impersonation of real, trusted people, real-time deepfakes, and the scale and personalisation that the technology brings to financial crime," he said.

AI technology allows criminals to produce deepfake videos of trusted people, including doctors, celebrities and business leaders, to promote fake products or investments. It can clone voices of family members, colleagues or executives asking for money.

The volume and quality of scam techniques are a concern, as large language models can write fluent, personalised messages in any language, with fewer spelling mistakes, and can run thousands of conversations at once.

"We used to tell people to look for spelling mistakes," Jha said, adding that advances in AI mean scammers can produce fluent, convincing messages with few obvious errors.

Scammers can appear on a live call impersonating someone else, Jha said, pointing to a 2024 case in Hong Kong, when United Kingdom engineering firm Arup transferred about HK$200m ($36.5 million) to criminals after a deepfaked multi-person conference.

"AI has turned scamming from a craft into a factory. A few seconds of your voice is now enough for a criminal to become you," he said.

Professor in CyberCrime and Cyberwar at UNSW, Richard Buckland, said any information available on the internet is accessible to criminals using AI, and that experts were "just scratching the surface" of its abilities.

"If I wanted to scam you, you might have published all sorts of stuff in your youth, your dad might have said things, your friends may have, but it's in a thousand locations, and before AI, no one would ever find it," he said

"But that's actually all inside the AI now. So AIs can access a vast amount of information about us and know about us."

AI lets criminals enact existing scams faster, at scale and more convincingly, he said, and the technology was easily accessible.

"It's really a world of outsourcing now; you could pay someone to do it, you could buy a model that does it."

The most common scams targeting businesses

The most common scams affecting businesses include the impersonation of legitimate business email accounts, known as Business Email Compromise (BEC), payment redirection scams, impersonation scams, mule accounts, identity fraud, investment scams and goods and services scams.

BEC and payment redirection scams involve criminals gaining access to or impersonating legitimate business email accounts. Victims often believe they are paying a genuine supplier or business partner, when the funds are being transferred to a fraudulent account.

Jha said scammers use AI to study a company’s public information, past emails where accounts have been compromised, and the writing style of its executives and suppliers. They then send a "perfectly worded email, in the right tone, at the right moment in a real transaction", asking to update banking details.

AI can also generate realistic fake invoices and receipts that match a supplier’s branding. "Instead of just an email, the 'CEO' now follows up with a phone call in their cloned voice, or joins a video call."

READ MORE Joseph knows how to fight scams. This one almost got to him

Similarly, scammers can pretend to be trusted organisations or individuals, including banks, suppliers or government agencies.

Impersonation scams generally rely on urgency and social conditioning to pressure victims to share information, click malicious links or approve payments or transfer funds.

One of the most significant emerging threats identified by ANZ is the use of stolen or falsified identities to open accounts that can receive scam proceeds. Known as "mule" accounts, these are used to facilitate financial crime, including money laundering.

Identity fraud was the most common scam reported in 2025, and ANZ said it has identified a "growing misuse" of mule accounts across the financial system.

Investment scams trick individuals and businesses into investing in fake or non-existent opportunities by promising attractive returns or exclusive offers. They rank consistently among the highest-loss scam categories reported to ANZ.

"AI easily produces deepfake videos of well-known business figures, journalists or politicians endorsing a trading platform, fake news articles, fake dashboards showing ‘profits’, and chatbots that keep victims engaged for weeks," Jha said.

"In short, AI removes the tell-tale signs we taught people to look for: bad grammar, a stranger’s voice, a generic greeting. The scam now looks and sounds like business as usual."

Individuals and businesses are also urged to look out for goods and services scams — advertised goods and services that are fake, misrepresented or never delivered after payment is made, commonly occurring through online marketplaces, social media platforms and fraudulent websites. While often lower in value, goods and services scams remain among the highest-volume scam types reported by ANZ.

ANZ general manager specialist sales, Cosi De Angelis, said that as AI evolved, financial crime was becoming harder to detect because it is "often hidden within legitimate businesses, trusted relationships, and everyday transactions".

"In many cases, criminals are exploiting trust as effectively as they are technology," De Angelis said.

How to defend against 'routine' scams

Jha said that scams would only become more sophisticated.

"We'll see real-time deepfake video calls become routine, AI agents that run entire scam conversations end to end, and scams that combine stolen data, cloned voices and fake documents in one coordinated attack," he said.

"It is an arms race, and criminals adapt quickly to every new defence."

Between October 2025 and June 2026, ANZ customer scam losses fell by 24 per cent compared with the same period the previous year. During that time, the bank said it also prevented and recovered more than $100 million in scam and fraud-related funds.

ANZ said it is encouraging businesses to review their cyber security practices and ensure staff understand the warning signs of cyber-enabled scams and fraud.

"Technology will continue to evolve, but human judgement remains one of the strongest defences," De Angelis said.

Jha said there was real progress being made by banks, telcos and digital platforms using AI to detect and prevent cybercrime.

"Reported losses have come down from their peak in recent years. Banks are also intercepting and recovering more stolen money than before. That shows coordinated action works," he said.

But Buckland said in the meantime, large financial institutions needed to stop contacting customers by phone and email.

"If you get an email, there's actually no way you can absolutely be sure it's the right email. And if we get a call, there's no way we can be sure we're speaking to who we think we are, even if the correct number shows on the screen.

"So companies have to stop doing it," he said.

While banks were "lucky" to have physical branches, Buxton anticipated acting against these threats would be a problem for many organisations, in a future where the only trustworthy communications would be "in-person".

"If you can only contact your customers electronically, you can no longer be distinguished from a scammer," he said.

"So how's it going to work?"

title: 'Voice of the news': Tributes continue for former SBS host Richard Morecroft
text:
IN BRIEF Richard Morecroft has died aged 70, after sharing his cancer diagnosis in July 2026.

Morecroft spent almost twenty years leading the ABC's 7pm NSW news bulletin.

Former ABC News presenter and SBS host Richard Morecroft has been remembered as a generational talent.

Morecroft died "at a time of his choosing" on NSW's south coast on Tuesday, aged 70, following his cancer diagnosis earlier in 2026, his family said.

"We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," they wrote in a statement shared via Morecroft's Instagram page.

Morecroft moved from England to Australia aged 10, studying at the University of Adelaide before taking a post at the ABC via the university's radio station.

He presented ABC's South Australian news bulletin before moving to Sydney, where he went on to host the network's 7pm NSW news bulletin from 1983 to 2002.

'A beloved part of Australian life'

title: Coalition's 'biggest' ever migration slashing has three major issues, critic says
text:
Key Points Net overseas migration would be cut to 100,000, almost a third of current levels.

The plan flags new cuts to temporary visas for graduates, low-skill migrants and humanitarian intake.

The Coalition has pledged the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history", slashing migrant numbers by more than 100,000.

Prioritising "high-value" migrants over family members and international students, halving humanitarian visas, while also cracking down on visa hopping and overstayers, has been branded a policy grounded on "three false premises" that could damage the economy, by a migration expert.

Coalition leader Angus Taylor says the plan will reduce temporary visa holders by around 650,000 over four years, and deliver a budget-neutral outcome while reducing overall migrant numbers by replacing lower-tax-paying temporary migrants with higher-skilled workers.

"If you have a temporary graduate visa or a student visa, on average, they’re going to give you $7,000 to $14,000 of tax income and economic contribution," Taylor said on Tuesday. "A temporary skilled visa is over $30,000."

Net overseas migration (NOM) will fall to almost a third of current levels, reducing the 3 million temporary migrants in Australia by tightening visa application pathways to stop visa-hopping by international students who use it to become temporary permanent migrants. Overseas arrivals would be linked to housing completions in Australia, which were 170,000 last year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We have seen under Labor our universities selling not education but visa pathways, migration pathways. That will end under this policy," Taylor said.

"We will bring in higher-skilled migrants who better meet Australia’s needs. This means prioritising skilled migration, including skilled partners and employer-sponsored applicants who meet high-quality criteria for income, age, English and full-time work."

Source: SBS News

Assuring voters the cuts to immigration would not add to skills shortages, a specialist stream of the Skills in Demand Visa will bring in up to 5,000 more highly skilled workers each year, and 15,000 Skilled Project Visas each year will be added for major projects, with workers tied to a defined project and period to plug workforce shortages.

Business groups, Labor and Greens push back

However, business groups, Labor and the Greens agree the cuts are too deep and will hurt the economy.

Property Council of Australia chief executive Mike Zorbas said the cuts will "tip a big bucket of cold water over businesses across Australia".

"Just when the Albanese government was busy proving they were best placed to tax the life out of investment in housing supply over the next year, along comes this flat tyre of a policy," Zorbas said.

"These migration cuts are just too deep for precision outcomes ... This limbo-dancing under One Nation’s migration bar will end in tears."

Greens Leader David Shoebridge told SBS News immigration policy needs to adapt for diaspora communities to connect via family reunions, a fair humanitarian intake can be matched with investments in TAFE and universities to meet Australian industry and skills needs.

“We are not going to start picking figures out of the air that fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. The proof is watching how One Nation, the Coalition and Labor have all been chopping and changing their number over the past 18 months as soon as serious scrutiny is applied," Shoebridge said.

Assistant Minister for Productivity Andrew Leigh told the ABC the proposed immigration changes will have a "huge negative impact on the economy".

The Coalition plan would virtually eliminate bridging visas. Protection visa applications will need to be made within 30 days of arrival and merit review rights for some visa refusals and character decisions will be removed.

Migration expert says plan based on 'false premises'

Changes to the temporary graduate visa were "clearly necessary", Australian National University professor Alan Gamlen, a migration expert, told SBS News.

"These were expanded for simple reasons: it doesn't make sense to have somebody come to Australia and pay to get an Australian degree, and just when they're ready to enter the labour market, having paid their own costs to get ready for it, we send them home," Gamlen said.

The visa was built for a post-pandemic labour market that was still recovering but those conditions no longer apply.

However, he said the Coalition's other changes are "One Nation lite", based on several "false premises" because countries as diverse as Austria, Czech Republic, Netherlands, and Canada face similar migration issues after their arrivals went down and then up after the pandemic.

"The (migration) policies put in place by the Coalition for very good reasons during the pandemic emergency were extended by the Labor government.. this was bipartisan, so it's not just a bipartisan problem; it's also a global problem," Gamlen said.

"Now, since the pandemic, the arrivals in aggregate have not grown. The departures have shrunk. That's the main thing that has contributed to the excess net overseas migration that we've experienced."

Cutting arrivals won't solve the problem of too few departures, but it will cause "significant harm to the economy" at the scale the Coalition is promising, he said.

Another problematic premise in their policy is the relationship between migration and housing, Gamlen said.

"Migration on the one hand ... drives demand for more housing, but migration is also partly the solution to the lack of housing because the housing construction supply chain needs more labour.

"House prices are actually going down at the moment, and that's because of something that's got nothing to do with migration."

Visa hopping led to low departures, creating a "guest worker society", a spokesperson for Taylor told SBS news.

"Our plan tackles visa hopping by requiring most temporary visa holders to apply for secondary or subsequent visa from offshore.

"Low departure rates have also been exacerbated by Labor's failure to address the over 70,000 unlawful non-citizens residing in Australia, as well as the 30,000 illegal boat arrivals Labor has failed to remove."

'Higher' migration standards

Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam said: "Lowering the numbers while lifting the standards isn't just a slogan".

“We’ve been putting in the work to ensure that what we announce actually won’t destroy the economy, like One Nation’s immigration plan will. And, of course, actually do something to lower the numbers. Unlike Labor’s plan," he told News24.

Nationals leader, Matt Canavan said the policy is "an Australia first migration plan".

"We’re not just a campground, we are a nation of borders, we’re not a booking.com site, and we owe Australians a living wage, not to have their salaries undermined by a cheap foreign labour force," Canavan said.

Second and third-year Working Holiday Makers will be able to reapply onshore, reversing Labor’s ballot system and caps for second- and third-year Working Holiday Maker visa extensions.

Taylor said the Coalition will differentiate between Working Holiday Makers in regional and non-regional areas by raising visa fees with an exemption for regional areas.

However, second and subsequent temporary visa applications will need to be made offshore, to reduce visa hopping.

The plan will also halve the humanitarian intake to 10,000 places a year, but remain flexible to respond to crisis needs.

What are Labor and One Nation's immigration policy alternatives?

Labor: Changes announced in September will make it harder and more expensive for international students to change visas, stop them from bringing family members and reduce backpacker numbers by 40,000 to get the NOM down to 225,000 by 2028.

Labor also announced a crackdown on visa overstayers and migration agents lodging baseless claims.

There are also reforms to the migration points system tipping the balance towards people with housing construction, healthcare, and education skills.

One Nation: After announcing a NOM figure of "about 130,000", the party settled on "negative migration", followed by an annual NOM figure of 130,000 people.

It plans to "cut immigration by over 570,000 people from current Labor levels" by capping visas at 130,000 per year to ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure. And deport any visa holder who breaks the law. Introduce an eight-year waiting period for citizenship and welfare, ensuring new arrivals contribute before they take.

title: Comedian Judith Lucy announces cancer diagnosis: 'I'll be keeping you abreast'
text:
IN BRIEF Comedian Judith Lucy has announced she will undergo a double mastectomy following a breast cancer diagnosis.

She shared the news in a joke-filled video, quipping about the ironic timing of her newly released book on wellness.

Judith Lucy has been diagnosed with breast cancer and will undergo a double mastectomy in the coming weeks.

The Australian comedian and actress announced the news in a video posted on social media on Tuesday, joking that she learned of the diagnosis shortly after receiving a faecal transplant and just before releasing her new book, Well Well Well.

"Now let's address the elephant in the room ... there's nothing like releasing a book on wellness as you're being diagnosed with breast cancer," she quipped.

She said the cancer was "relatively non-aggressive" and in its early stages, and she had decided to remove both breasts after her doctor recommended a single mastectomy.

"I have had 40 years of, if I do say so myself, large and spectacular breasts. You had your chance, fellas," she said.

"I'll be keeping you abreast of everything, Australia."

Lucy's decades-long comedy career

title: The two-metre question that could wipe out a population
text:
IN BRIEF World leaders will spend a day on Tuvalu's main atoll as part of the pre-COP31 summit.

The summit has drawn criticism on several fronts, including the sparse turnout of leaders beyond the Pacific.

Leaders from 13 countries will join Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Tuvalu's capital, Funafuti, today to see what rising seas are doing to one of the world's lowest-lying nations.

The country, which is made up of three islands, sits on average just two metres above sea-level, with the highest point reaching just 4.6 metres above sea-level.

The visit is the centrepiece of the pre-COP31 summit, the annual meeting at which ministers set priorities for United Nations climate negotiations.

Fiji is co-hosting the four-day gathering in Nadi with Tuvalu and Australia, a role Pacific nations secured through a compromise that gave COP31 hosting rights to Türkiye and the position of president of negotiations to Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.

Pre-COPs are usually low-key meetings of ministers and officials, but the Australian government invited national leaders to Tuvalu to see the threat of climate change up close.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The delegation will fly more than 1,000 kilometres north from Fiji, joined by UN climate chief Simon Stiell, European Union climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum.

They will travel by canoe to inspect land raised under the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project and solar projects built to cut the country's reliance on diesel, before returning to Fiji to sign a leaders' declaration.

"We ask you to come to the Pacific because some things cannot be understood from a distance," Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka told delegates on Monday.

Sea level rise a 'present reality' for Tuvalu

NASA's Sea Level Change Team found sea levels around Tuvalu rose about 15 centimetres in the three decades to 2023 — roughly one and a half times the global average.

The team projects that much of the country's land and critical infrastructure will lie below the average high-tide mark by 2050.

Seawater is already seeping into soil and freshwater supplies, making taro and breadfruit harder to grow, while bleaching degrades the corals that sustain the country's fisheries.

"Sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly last month.

About 60 per cent of Tuvalu's roughly 10,000 people live on Funafuti.

Under the 2023 Falepili Union treaty, Australia offers up to 280 Tuvaluans permanent residency each year.

Registrations for the first visa ballot in 2025, including family members, covered more than a third of the population.

The first recipients arrived earlier this year.

A thin international guest list

Only one national leader from outside the Pacific is expected to make the trip to the pre-COP31 event, triggering the Opposition to criticise the government over the value of the summit.

Fiji had named five leaders from beyond the region as likely attendees, but some have withdrawn, including Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul as severe flooding hit Bangkok.

Diplomats from several Western nations told Reuters they could not justify a multi-day journey with COP31 only weeks away.

READ MORE The climate question following Albanese from Palau to New York

For Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu, the turnout fell short: "We were hoping for more," he told Reuters.

Bowen defended the numbers, citing the president of Palau's view that "if you get one prime minister, you're doing well because prime ministers and presidents don't go to pre-COP".

Opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson Dan Tehan argued the low attendance showed the conference was a waste of taxpayers' money, calling it a "farce" and Bowen's "vanity project".

Hosts under scrutiny over fossil fuel records

Environmental groups and Pacific nations have both criticised the two COP31 hosts over their record on combating climate change.

The summit opened days after a NSW regulator approved a 19-year extension of the Hunter Valley Operations coal mine, the largest coal mine expansion in the state's history.

Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the extension could produce 809 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval.

In September, Regenvanu said Australia wasn't doing enough to lower greenhouse gas emissions, saying "the very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that".

Climate Analytics chief executive Bill Hare said Labor had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022.

Using UN trade data, a 350.org report estimated Australian coal shipped to Türkiye had been responsible for more than 75 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since 2015.

"Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates," 350.org's head of political strategy Andreas Sieber said.

Australia accounts for 25 per cent of world coal exports, ranking second behind Indonesia for total coal exports among all nations, according to the International Energy Agency.

Türkiye drew 33.6 per cent of its electricity from coal last year, according to official figures, despite a 2053 net-zero target.

In July, a Turkish court struck down environmental approval for two new units at the Afşin-Elbistan lignite plant.

A month earlier, the government announced a new 1,050-megawatt unit at the Cenal coal plant, according to campaign group Beyond Fossil Fuels.

title: UK author, former Conservative MP Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
text:
In brief Author Jeffrey Archer has died shortly before the release of his final novel.

His careers as an author and politician were marked by literary success and scandal.

Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged ‌86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Tuesday.

Archer sold more over 300 million copies of his books worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers ‌such as his 1976 debut Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less and 1979's Kane & Abel. His final novel, Adam and Eve, is due to be published on Tuesday.

Kate Elton, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor, said in a statement: "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend."

Archer was also ‌a prominent Conservative politician, ‌who served ⁠as an MP for five years before becoming a senior party official under then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.

But he was as well-known for his very public downfall.

title: 'My whole life is here': Australians fear being forced overseas to care for ageing parents
text:
In Brief: Families say new visitor visa rules will make it harder to reunite with ageing parents.

Parent visa applicants face waits of up to 18 years, and more than 40 years in some cases.

Jen's mother died waiting for her Australian visa to be approved.

Now, eight years after first lodging an application, she fears her widowed father could be left in limbo too.

Jen moved from South Africa in 2008 as an international student. Since then, she's built a life in Australia, married, had children and became a citizen.

Thinking about the future, she applied for a Contributory Parent visa in 2018 so her parents could eventually join her in Australia.

Her mother died in 2022 before the visa was processed — and eight years on, her father is still waiting.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the meantime, he's travelled regularly between South Africa and Australia to spend time with Jen and his grandchildren. But changes to visitor rules mean even that may soon become harder.

"It really impacts our family because we don't have multi-generational care and family around, and my parents don't know my kids as intimately as we wish they would," Jen told SBS News.

The changes were announced in September as part of the federal government's efforts to reduce net overseas migration.

Among them was a new "no further stay" condition that will be applied to visitor visas, preventing holders from applying for another visa while in Australia.

For Australians with ageing parents living overseas, advocates say it removes one of the few practical pathways that allowed families to stay together while waiting for parent visas that can take decades to process.

Now, Jen faces a choice she never expected to make.

"Our whole life is here," she said.

"So if we want to reunite with my dad, I have to move the whole family over either back to South Africa with my Australian kids and my Australian husband and then restart our lives there, or we do this long-distance family thing."

'No further stay'

The "no further stay" condition requires visitor visa holders to leave Australia before applying for another visa.

The government says the measure will ensure visitor visas "are only used by genuine visitors and not as a pathway to extending a stay in Australia" and is aimed at curbing so-called visa hopping.

But Melbourne-based registered migration agent Gary Grewal says the change is affecting families who were never the target.

Until now, parents who met the age requirements could enter Australia on a visitor visa, apply for a parent visa from within Australia and remain in the country on a bridging visa while waiting for a decision.

"Now with the no further stay condition, they cannot apply for these visas," he said. "So the reality is they need to go back and wait overseas."

Registered migration agent Gary Grewal says the government's visitor visa change is affecting families who were never the target. Source: Supplied / Gary Grewal

Grewal said visitor visas granted to parents have also become more restrictive in recent years.

Where parents were previously able to spend extended periods in Australia, more recent visas have often been granted for significantly shorter stays, further reducing the time families can spend together.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said in July that the parent visa backlog was something the government was working to address, but there were no easy answers.

In the 2024-25 financial year, there were 157,000 parent visas in the backlog, an increase of 52,000 compared to six years ago, according to Department of Home Affairs data.

Waits that outlast the applicants

The changes come against a backdrop of lengthy parent visa queues.

The Contributory Parent visa, which costs about $49,000, has an estimated processing time of 18 years.

The much cheaper Aged Parent visa, available to eligible parents who have reached pension age, has an estimated processing time of more than 42 years.

For Jen, those figures have become painfully personal as her father ages.

"Even though we're in the queue, we can't have my dad stay here and just wait it out until the visa's granted," she said.

"If you do the maths, your parent has to be 109 years old to get that visa.

"There's no human filter to these policies that they're putting in place."

Almost half of Australians have at least one parent born overseas, according to 2021 Census data.

Grewal said annual caps on parent visas have contributed to growing queues, leaving families separated for years or even decades.

"It's a big toll on the family for what you want to do, which is spend time with your ageing parents," Jen said.

An impossible choice

For Sandhya, the problem isn't immediate, but she's worried it soon could be.

She moved from the United States to Western Australia about a decade ago. She and her partner are now Australian citizens and have built their lives here with their children.

Her parents, who live in India and are aged in their 70s and 80s, are healthy and active.

But she always assumed that if one of them became seriously ill, lost their partner or could no longer live independently, there would be a pathway to bring them to Australia.

Now she is no longer sure.

"It only takes a fall or an illness or a loss of one of them for the situation to become really urgent and for me to want to bring them here permanently," she said.

"The only option is for us to apply for an aged parent visa, but that's going to take decades.

"One or two years is a reasonable time, but what is with 10 to 20 years? If you're applying for your parents, are you expecting them to live to 150?"

Sandhya said she and her partner have paid almost $2 million in taxes since arriving in Australia and would happily support their parents financially if they came.

"For us to not have any pathway to bring our parents here, that's a very worrying prospect," she said. "So what is the solution for me?"

"I would have to move back to India, but my kids are building their lives here."

The cost to families

Grewal said the loss of bridging visa pathways means family reunification is increasingly becoming dependent on wealth and circumstance.

He points to one Perth family who withdrew a parent visa application because they could not afford the costs involved.

When the father later suffered a serious accident in India, his son had to leave Australia to care for him.

Debates around migration have dominated Australian politics of late, with the government unveiling their long-awaited policy in September. Source: AAP / Dean Lewins

Another couple, a GP and a psychiatrist who had lived in Australia for 15 years, ultimately relocated to India permanently to be with their ageing parents.

"It is very difficult," he said. "Families are going to be split for at least a decade."

"Grandparents can't see their grandchildren. They can't help with their children's families."

Grewal believes Australia risks losing skilled migrants to countries that provide faster and more practical options for family reunification.

Sandhya wants the government to look more closely at the human impact of migration policy and rejects the narrative that immigrants are "resource-hungry".

"People from other countries are legitimate contributors to society here, and we have to find pathways for when they're in a vulnerable state and need support."
