title: Spain's prime minister calls early election after housing crisis triggers mass protests
text:
In brief Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for November 29.

It comes after tens of thousands of protesters marched across Spain over the weekend.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Monday for 29 November, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.

The defeat on Friday was just the latest political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the left still in power.

"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".

Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The defeat infuriated those protesting the country's increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.

Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez's government, for several years.

The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.

Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.

Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.

Soaring prices

Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.

Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 per cent, according to real estate website Idealista.

Abascal's eviction catalysed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.

The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 per cent, according to housing campaigners.

The backlash led the new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.

The housing bills Sanchez's leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts — on whose support the government relies — voted against them, arguing they were hastily drawn up and would make the housing crisis worse.

'Can take no more'

Sanchez defended his government's record in his address, pointing out that under his leadership Spain's economy has grown faster than those of its main European peers.

But after eight years in power, Sanchez is also under pressure from corruption scandals involving people close to him, including his wife and top figures in his Socialist Party.

The prime minister has also faced widespread criticism over his handling of the crisis in the north African enclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants from Morocco entered in late July.

The situation at the European land border with Africa has gradually deteriorated, with many migrants still sleeping in makeshift camps.

The events have fuelled tensions and almost daily protests by local residents calling for a return to normality.

The head of the PP, Alberto Nunez Feijóo, again called on Sanchez on Saturday to call an election, saying the country "can take no more".

While polls put the PP ahead, they suggest the party would fall short of an absolute majority in parliament and would need the support of far-right Vox to govern.

title: Australia's illegal tobacco boom is taking a heavy toll. But new data offers a glimmer of hope
text:
In brief The peak body for the convenience industry is calling on the government to cut the tobacco excise.

It comes as new data from Queensland shows a jump in legal cigarette sales after new enforcement laws took effect.

Convenience store owners across Australia are being threatened, attacked and extorted as the illegal tobacco trade strips billions from legal cigarette sales, the industry's peak body says.

Owners have lost $3 billion in legal cigarette sales in the past five years, according to the Australian Association of Convenience Stores chief executive Theo Foukkare.

"Some of our members are being stood over, threatened and asked to pay protection money. They have been ram-raided, they have been held up at gunpoint," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

"The safety of the 80,000 frontline staff that our members employ around the country has gone backwards."

Foukkare is among dozens of industry experts and economists calling on the federal government to slash the tobacco excise, as Labor insists the tax is a good thing and urges states to crack down on illegal trade.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Legal cigarette sales jump in Queensland

Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill has pointed to data out of Queensland to bolster the arguments.

The state's legal tobacco sales rose 55 per cent in the first month after new enforcement laws took effect in November and remained at least 40 per cent above previous levels for the next six months, data supplied by major retailers to the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner shows.

Nationally, the market remained almost flat across the same time period.

"We cannot overstate the emphasis on shutting down retail premises that are blatantly selling illegal products in high streets," Hill told AAP.

Foukkare said a roaring underground trade meant sales of legal cigarettes in Queensland were still well below what they were five years ago.

In other states, the picture was even bleaker.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said his state had successfully begun closing shops selling tobacco without a licence, yet crime was moving to the streets.

"We're actually seeing them now trying to change their business model. So this is why we do need to be one step ahead," he told reporters on Monday.

Foukkare said Queensland's success was likely because it had shut down illegal stores in blitz suburbs and beyond, meaning people needed to drive large distances for illegal products.

However, people were now using WhatsApp and meet-ups to sell cigarettes.

Modelling from Tulipwood Economics, commissioned by the association, showed that freezing the excise and legalising but regulating smoking cessation tools like nicotine pouches would generate $6.2 billion in GST over four years.

READ MORE The dramatic shift in a longstanding Australian addiction

"It's time for you [the government] to change your position on tobacco control policy because you have absolutely failed everybody in Australia on this," Foukkare said.

"Stop being so pig-headed and stuck in ideology."

Government resists calls to slash excise

The Coalition has vowed to slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent if elected, dropping the average price of cigarettes from between $50 and $40 to roughly $16-$26.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor said the cut would take the oxygen out of the thriving black market, which he called "economic terrorism".

"Our strong plan will attack the gangs where it hurts by taking away their massive price advantage, taking away their customers, and taking away their profits," he said.

One Nation wants to slash the tax by 75 per cent and freeze indexation for five years.

NSW Premier Chris Minns has long advocated for an excise cut.

Hill waved away the criticism, accusing the Coalition of being in "some crazy bidding war" with One Nation.

Queensland-based calls to Quitline, a national hotline for smokers trying to quit, more than doubled in the days following large enforcement operations, which he said indicated the crackdown was causing some smokers to quit.

"This is a really positive by-product of strong enforcement at the retail level," Hill said.

Public health groups have warned that cutting the excise and making tobacco cheaper could reverse decades of decline in smoking rates and have serious ramifications for the health of Australians.

Durban: Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg has revealed he told curators at major venues to prepare flatter pitches for this summer and beyond, amid fears about a recent spate of two-day Test matches that have damaged the game’s finances. Whatever the success or failure of the pre-COP meeting in Fiji, it is clear the Albanese government will wear a political cost for putting it on. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, left, with former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern in Nadi, Fiji, on Wednesday. This way Australia could rattle the can for donations to the region from far-flung nations for the eye-bleeding cost of climate mitigation in the Pacific, elevate its climate concerns, and show off the damage already done to low-lying nations to demonstrate the immediate threat of climate change.

With a budget in deficit and interest rates climbing, Australian voters are getting twitchy with the government spending their tax money on their own needs, let alone those of their regional neighbours. title: Home construction is up but still well short of government targets
text:
Advertisement

A surge in homes built last quarter has failed to get the government back on track for its 1.2 million homes target as experts warn the deteriorating economic conditions threaten to slow down future housing projects. The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its quarterly building activity data on Wednesday, showing a boost to the number of homes that began construction and the number of projects finished in the June quarter. But it also showed Labor remained almost 100,000 short of the homes needed to reach its target of building a record number of dwellings over five years – a key plank in its plan to tackle the housing crisis and get more first home buyers into the market. Housing commencements and completions surged in the last quarter. Sitthixay Ditthavong The number of homes, including houses and apartments, that began construction in the June quarter rose 7 per cent to 52,201. Homes that were completed rose 5.8 per cent to 47,168.

Advertisement

But the home building sector has this year been hit by a series of interest rate hikes, higher construction prices due to the Middle East war and uncertainty prompted by the May budget’s housing tax changes which are yet to properly flow through to the figures. KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said the uptick in commencements and completions showed Australia was trending in the right direction, and a record number of more than 240,000 houses under construction would enter the market over the next year or so. “Developers are seeing that prices are softening, their holding costs are increasing... so they’re probably on the bike pedalling as fast as they can to complete projects and get them into the market,” he said. But projects starting today would be more expensive because they break ground after the start of the US’s war on Iran, which has increased oil costs, he said.

Advertisement

“This is probably as good as it’s going to get for the foreseeable future,” he said. Housing Industry Association chief economist Tim Reardon said the 52,000 commencements in the quarter would not be enough to keep up with demand. “There hasn’t been a material increase in the volume of new home building over the past decade, we’re still building a similar volume … despite the pick-up that we can see in today’s data, it’s about average for recent decades,” he said. “We have not built enough homes in the past year to meet growth and demand, and we don’t anticipate that in the next 12 months we’ll build enough homes to meet the growth in demand.”

Advertisement

Reardon said the number of houses would probably continue to rise in the September quarter because of the strength of the market coming into 2026, but they could start to fall by early 2027. Related Article Property prices It will take a generation to fix the housing crisis, says top economist “What today’s data shows us is just how much momentum there was in the housing market coming into this year,” he said. “That growth isn’t going to be sustained, and that we won’t see an increase in home building activity in 2027.” The association estimates the failure to hit the government’s housing targets has left an $11 billion “black hole” in the finances of state and territory governments because not enough stamp duty and GST was collected over the two years since the target was set. Had the target been on track, the construction would have generated $45 billion in economic activity and potentially housed 242,160 Australians based on average household sizes, the housing association said.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said there was still more work to do on housing construction. Louie Douvis Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Housing Minister Clare O’Neil released a statement on Wednesday welcoming the June quarter increase in dwelling starts and completions. “These are encouraging numbers, but we know they can bounce around from quarter to quarter and that there’s more work to do,” it said. “We are tackling housing supply from all angles, including funding enabling infrastructure, building 55,000 social and affordable homes and working with states and territories to streamline approvals.” Master Builders Australia chief executive Denita Wawn said the outlook for new projects was increasingly challenging.

“The cumulative impact of the federal budget, continued interest rate increases and an ongoing global uncertainty have deteriorated the environment.” She said the “flat result” for higher density housing revealed by the latest figures was concerning because strong growth in that type of residential construction was needed it Australia is meet its housing targets. title: ‘A mystery’: The men fuelling Victoria’s record drug overdose toll
text:

Fatal overdoses among Gen X men have increased by almost 50 cent in Victoria in a single year, driving the state’s drug-related deaths to their highest levels since the heroin glut of the late 1990s. A new Coroner’s Court report shows 632 overdose fatalities were recorded in Victoria last year – the highest number since the court began collecting data in 2000. New Coroner’s Court data shows a marked increase in overdose deaths among men aged 45–54. Istock Men aged 45 to 54 were more likely to die from a drug overdose than any other age group, with the number of deaths in this cohort rising from 106 in 2024 to 156 last year – a rise of 47 per cent. The report said it was not known what was driving the rise among this age group.

“An increase of 50 [fatal overdoses] in a single cohort in one year has not been observed in any other group for the reporting period,” the report said. John Ryan, chief executive of public health research and drug policy organisation the Penington Institute, said the unprecedented rise in deaths among Gen X men was “a bit of a mystery” that needed further investigation. Ryan said he suspected that GPs becoming more cautious about prescribing addictive drugs, as well as real-time prescription monitoring, had led to middle-aged men previously addicted to pharmaceutical drugs being pushed into Victoria’s illicit drug market. “There’s a possibility that people have shifted from pharmaceutical misuse to illicit drug use. title: ‘Groundbreaking’: High Court quashes coal mine expansion over climate emissions
text:
Advertisement

Approval for a major coal mine expansion has been declared invalid by the High Court in a decision that will force NSW planning authorities to reckon with emissions from Australian coal burnt overseas. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government was still considering the 111-page judgment handed down on Wednesday, while casting doubt on whether the decision would set a national precedent. Heavy machinery working at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant Coal Mine Operations near Muswellbrook. Kate Geraghty But the federal opposition is demanding the Albanese government intervene should the NSW Labor government fail to urgently pass new laws. One Nation deputy leader Barnaby Joyce echoed the call for new legislation, arguing that the court decision would make Australia poorer. “Poorer nations cannot pay for the public infrastructure and the social security benefits that are part of the birthright of this nation,” Joyce said. The NSW government has been contacted for comment.

Advertisement

Anita Hart, a lawyer for the local environment group fighting the project, celebrated the victory, calling it “a groundbreaking decision for climate law in Australia” that would be studied closely by other countries. Related Article Mining Courts turn on coal mines over climate impacts The Greens’ new deputy federal leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it would send a clear message to both government and business that “when Australian coal is burnt overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port”. The case revolved around an open-cut coal mine at Mount Pleasant in the NSW Hunter region, a political battleground eyed by both the Coalition and One Nation. Owner MACH Energy Australia won approval in 2022 to significantly expand the mine and extend its life by 22 years. It outlined measures to address domestic greenhouse gas emissions from the project.

Advertisement

But it also concluded that 98 per cent of the total emissions would be classed as “scope 3”, a category for further use of a product, such as the burning of coal for energy after export. The owner argued these emissions would be managed “in accordance with customer countries commitments under the Paris Agreement” and would not “contribute to Australian greenhouse gas emissions”. Neither the NSW Department Planning and Environment nor the ultimate decision maker, the Independent Planning Commission, took issue with the company’s position. The mine owner survived one legal challenge from environmentalists known as Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group Inc, before the tables then turned in the NSW Court of Appeal. The High Court on Wednesday upheld the lower court’s decision, but on a different basis.

Advertisement

Under NSW law, the Independent Planning Commission needed to consider imposing conditions on an approval to ensure “that greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable”. Justice James Edelman said: “Members of the Commission did not address that requirement with respect to scope 3 emissions, amounting to 98 per cent of the project’s emissions, because they considered that those emissions would be accounted for in the countries to which the coal was exported.” Edelman continued that “by focusing only upon two per cent of the project’s emissions”, the commission had failed to in its duty to fully consider minimisation conditions. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government was still working out the impacts of the decision. Alex Ellinghausen Justice Michelle Gordon said it was not the High Court’s role to weigh in on the merits of this requirement or to say what conditions might be imposed to minimise emissions. But Gordon found the failure to at least consider conditions was a “material” error that invalidated the expansion approval. Justice Robert Beech-Jones agreed.

Advertisement

Two other judges, Chief Justice Stephen Gageler and Justice Jayne Jagot, disagreed with the majority in finding that the planning commission had adequately considered emissions overseas. They quoted the commission’s finding that “with the adoption of the Paris Agreement, almost all countries have committed to reduce global [greenhouse gas] emissions and to track their progress in doing so”. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the government had not had an opportunity to read the judgment in full, but its early assessment was the impact would be limited to NSW. “It doesn’t automatically transfer to Commonwealth decisions or Commonwealth legislation,” Watt told News24 shortly after the decision was handed down. Watt reiterated that scope 3 emissions did not need to be considered under federal law, but said other states may be impacted depending on their legislative settings.

Advertisement

In a joint statement released on Wednesday afternoon, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Nationals leader Matt Canavan described the decision as “absurd”, seeking to blame Labor for the ruling. “The decision turns on the wording of NSW planning law. That means it can be fixed, and fixed quickly. The Coalition calls on the Minns government to act immediately to introduce legislation amending the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act. “It must make clear that overseas emissions from Australia’s exported resources are not a consideration in project approvals,” the Coalition leaders said. “If the NSW state government won’t act, the Albanese Labor government should legislate to fix this issue and provide certainty to workers, business and our international energy partners.”

title: Mary Fowler’s latest decision tells us something we should already know about her
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportSoccerMatildas Mary Fowler’s latest decision tells us something we should already know about her Vince Rugari October 7, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When someone shows you who they are, as American writer and civil rights activist Maya Angelou once said, you should believe them the first time. Mary Fowler has shown us who she is. She is not exactly hiding it. She has told us, explicitly and proudly, about what makes her tick, the things that she truly values in life, and where soccer sits in her personal pecking order – and we admire her for this. But we don’t seem to be listening. Loading We are patiently waiting for her to finally find that permanent role in the Matildas’ starting XI so that we can watch her settle in and play there for the next decade. We dream of seeing her become an undisputed global superstar, winning Ballons d’Or and UEFA Champions League medals, leading the Matildas and Australian soccer towards greatness, all without wondering if she actually wants any of these things, or if we just want them for us, via her. Fowler is reportedly back in Sydney visiting her partner, Penrith Panthers NRL star Nathan Cleary, as he recovers from a career-threatening broken leg. These are presumably the unexplained “personal circumstances” that led to her pulling out of the Matildas’ friendlies against Germany and Haiti – but since nothing has been said officially, we still don’t know for sure.

Advertisement

Regardless, coach Joe Montemurro has been denied a critical opportunity to advance his preparations for next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup, insofar as where Fowler fits into those plans. These are not “only friendlies”; this team will have just a handful of games together before the tournament begins, and Fowler has rarely been fully fit since Montemurro began in the job in June 2025. She is such a special player, Australia’s World Cup hopes rest at least partly on her shoulders. It exposes a tension between the inherent collective demands of international soccer and individual autonomy to decide what matters most in a player’s life. Mary Fowler and Nathan Cleary. Instagram In Fowler’s case, it forces us to confront the possibility that her idea of her career might look very different to ours. “Obviously I enjoy playing football, but I wouldn’t say it’s my passion,” Fowler said last year on the Keegan and Company podcast, recorded in the days after she underwent surgery on her ACL.

Advertisement

When she was much younger, soccer was her “everything”, she explained. These days, it’s just her job. That doesn’t mean she’s not committed – obviously, she is – but it helps us understand her perspective. “I play it because there are a lot of things I enjoy about it,” she said. “I really enjoy travelling, being with my teammates, the people that I’ve met through football, but if I finished it tomorrow, I probably wouldn’t have any regrets. There’s other things outside of football I am more passionate about.” Mary Fowler on the ball for the Matildas in June. Getty Images It would be totally understandable, then, for Fowler to want to be by Cleary’s side at a time of serious trauma, and for that to outweigh her desire to play. If Fowler or Football Australia had confirmed this was why she wasn’t available for the Matildas, many people would have congratulated her for setting boundaries. She went even deeper on these topics in her book, Bloom, released last year, in which she detailed her thought process during the last time she withdrew from a Matildas camp, in late 2024. She publicly cited “physical and mental fatigue” – and she was applauded for her bravery – but when she first approached the team to ask for some time off, “the response wasn’t as supportive as I’d hoped,” she wrote.

Advertisement

Fowler was told it would not be a good look, that the Matildas risked the appearance of “favouritism” and that it could open a “can of worms” within the squad. “Although I noted the amount of pressure being put on me to still come in, I’m glad I stood firm in my decision,” she wrote. Mary Fowler is only 23, but has a maturity well beyond her age. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I made it known that, with all due respect, I was going to do what was best for me. There was a lot that didn’t sit well with me in the way those discussions were handled, but eventually I was given approval to pull out of the camp. I didn’t enjoy feeling like I was a commodity, but I understood that sometimes that’s just the ruthless side of business … no matter what pressures or backlash you face, you shouldn’t feel guilty for making yourself a priority.” Fowler is still only 23, but has a maturity well beyond her age. This is someone who meditates, who journals, who has thought all of this through, football and life, at a deeper level, and determined that the former is just a small part of the latter.

Advertisement

Honestly, good for her. Many people go through their entire lives without figuring this stuff out. But multiple things can be true at once: that Fowler is entitled to make the call she believes is right for herself, and that others, including her teammates, coaches and Matildas supporters, don’t have to love it. This is, as she put it, the ruthless side of the business. The Australian jersey is not a mere work uniform, but a representation of something much larger than the person wearing it: of fans who have emotionally invested in this team precisely for these reasons; of players and staff who accept that pursuing a common goal sometimes requires putting the collective above themselves; of every other aspiring footballer who would drop everything for the chance to pull it on, even just once. There is a reason it is referred to as “international duty.” It is a duty. When you have been selected to play for your country, availability is supposed to be the default position.

Advertisement

Of course, soccer does not come before everything, and there are times when players are given leave on compassionate grounds. Related Article Updated

Friendlies ‘I only just found out’: Fowler’s Matildas teammates in the dark over sudden withdrawal But there are also times when players would rather be somewhere else for perfectly compelling personal reasons and turn up anyway, because representing your country demands a higher level of sacrifice. They routinely leave partners and children behind, surrender precious time at home, travel enormous distances, which put strain on their bodies and minds, and sometimes face pressure from the clubs who actually pay their day-to-day wages. Opinions will vary as to whether returning home to comfort an injured partner reaches this undefined threshold. Fowler is absolutely entitled to decide that soccer isn’t the most important thing in her life, but when it comes to choosing not to play for the Matildas, there could also be footballing consequences.

Advertisement

What could those consequences be? That’s a thorny question, and one for Montemurro and Football Australia to tackle as they see fit, depending on their discussions with Fowler, the feelings of the rest of the squad and balancing those against her status as a generational talent. Based on what she has told us about herself, Fowler may well accept any consequences as the price of her own peace of mind. And the rest of us should probably accept that, too. We can continue dreaming of everything Fowler might achieve in football, but we shouldn’t assume she shares all of those dreams with us.

title: Frenchie
text:
The allure of Frenchie is multi-faceted, but the drawcard that really matters is simple: value. Yes, the room is moody and vibey, and the menu is full of dishes that capture some of the current edible zeitgeist – a little bit French, a touch playful, mostly snacky. But the point of difference here is that everything costs $14.

Everything? Well, yes, practically everything. You can buy a bottle rather than one of the ($14) glasses of wine, and they serve basic soft drinks for less. You can add fries to certain dishes for an extra $7. But everything else – the cocktails, the caviar bumps, the oysters (three per serve), the steak – is $14.

Silky beetroot-cured salmon gravlax rests on foamy green sorrel sauce. Grilled duck breast comes drizzled with a l’orange sauce. Eggplant is cooked to a pleasing slump and smothered in a goat’s cheese sauce. Dishes may not blow your mind, but most are perfectly acceptable.

As for the vibe? The collective relief of a room full of people who know they can have this much fun, without worrying too much about the damage when the bill comes, is downright exhilarating.

Must order: A martini (or three), made with a touch of absinthe, served in a beautiful coupe.

Cumulus Inc. was one of the city’s first wine-bar-slash-restaurants, and an early pioneer of the familiar-but-fun dinner menu served in a stylish industrial space.

Head chef Hannah Holleran’s menu may not look particularly inventive or singular – then the food hits the table. There are dozens of tuna tartares in this city, but very few are this fresh, served in hefty cubes over goat’s curd and vibrant green peas spiked with mint. Tender agnolotti, filled with beetroot ricotta and garnished with walnuts and sage, makes for an excellent mid-course before a 1.3-kilogram lamb shoulder arrives, fall-apart tender and smothered in an almond and red pepper sauce.

Cumulus Inc. is not only the model from which some of Melbourne’s best restaurants took inspiration, it continues to shine brightly as a standard-bearer of great service, fantastic wine and approachable, exciting and delicious dining.

Good to know: Weekends at Cumulus feel frenetic. Try a 3pm lunch or Monday night dinner for a slightly more relaxed groove.

And what about the steaks? The menu offers a wide choice of cuts, charred over a wood grill and cooked to exactly the right temperature, every time.

Does Rockpool still have a place in our dining landscape? Almost certainly. For the business lunch, absolutely. To just have a reliably good steak and martini and not have to think too much? Well, there are certainly other options these days, but this isn’t a bad one, not by a mile.

Platina Resources has fired up the drill rig for a second time, kicking off an aircore drilling campaign at its Granite Well East prospect, which forms part of the company’s Mt McKenna gold project just 13 kilometres east of Laverton in Western Australia. The 53-hole, 3200-metre program is designed to follow up highly encouraging gold mineralisation hits from a previous campaign and will test strike continuity and the system’s lateral extent. The new work at Granite Well East follows an earlier phase-three program that unearthed multiple mineralised zones, including a notable one-metre hit of a hefty 7.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 40m. Several intercepts from that campaign either finished in mineralisation or near the bottom of the hole, hinting the system remains open at depth. Other encouraging results from the earlier drilling included a 4-metre section grading 1.11g/t gold from just 12m, associated with a strong arsenic anomaly and a separate 7-metre intercept going 0.61g/t gold from 36m that continued to the bottom of the hole. A further hole delivered 4m grading 0.93g/t gold from 52m, also ending at the bottom of the hole.

The deal, which closed in stages over three years, delivered a whopping US$14 million (AU$20M) into Platina’s coffers. Platina Resources managing director Dr Paul Polito said: “The results of the program will assist in determining the scale, continuity and significance of mineralisation and guide subsequent exploration, such as reverse circulation drilling or induced polarisation surveys.” The project’s address has a rich pedigree, sitting adjacent to Genesis Minerals’ 3.9-million-ounce Laverton project and just 20km north-east of Gold Fields’ 3.9-million-ounce Granny Smith gold mine. The Granite Well East target itself lies at what is interpreted to be the intersection of two major structural corridors, a setting often favourable for trapping gold-bearing fluids. Pornhub is switching explicit content back on for Australian iPhone and iPad users who have confirmed their age with Apple, seven months after its owner gutted the site in protest at the new age verification laws. Aylo, the Montreal-based company behind Pornhub, said on Wednesday that age-verified iOS users in Australia would now be served “a standard adult user experience”. The statement made no change for Android or desktop users. Pornhub’s Canadian parent company previously cut off Australian users rather than comply with age check laws. Getty Since March 9, when the eSafety Commissioner’s Age-Restricted Material Codes took effect, Aylo has served Australian visitors a stripped-back version of Pornhub. Explicit videos were replaced with podcasts, lifestyle segments and branded merchandise, as this masthead reported at the time. The codes require high-risk services such as Pornhub to check users are over 18 before showing them pornography. Breaches carry penalties of up to $49.5 million each.

Advertisement

Aylo’s reversal is largely on the back of updates to Apple’s settings. Since September, Australians have had to confirm they are adults, by scanning an identity document or using a credit card, before downloading 18+ apps or switching off certain safety settings. Apple’s web content filter and communication safety tools are switched on automatically for anyone who has not confirmed they are over 18. Scarlet Alliance chief executive Mish Pony and president Jenna Love. Simon Schluter “In our view, Apple’s Australian device-level age-verification update offers one of the strongest and hardest to circumvent protections currently available for helping prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content,” Aylo said in a statement from Alex Kekesi, its vice-president of brand and community. Aylo has argued for years that age checks belong on the device rather than on individual websites. It said this approach protected children “without requiring adults to surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites”, and avoided systems that could be dodged with a VPN.

Advertisement

Related Article Harassment The day porn turned off: Inside Australia’s high-stakes war with the adult industry Aylo did not say how Pornhub identifies which visitors have passed Apple’s check, or whether eSafety had approved the approach. Sex workers had warned the restrictions would cost them money. Scarlet Alliance, the national peak body for sex workers, told this masthead in March that blocking compliant sites would push viewers to offshore platforms that are less likely to check who appears in their videos or to take down content uploaded without consent. “That leaves sex workers not earning income from their content,” Mish Pony, the group’s chief executive, said at time, “with obvious flow-on effects – lower earnings and being pushed into working in ways that are less safe.” Wednesday’s change restores full access only for iPhone and iPad users who have confirmed their age with Apple.

Advertisement

The regulator stopped short of endorsing the move. An eSafety spokesperson said services could use a range of age-assurance methods as long as they could show those methods were “fair, accurate, robust and effective” and complied with Australian privacy law. “It remains the responsibility of individual services, including Aylo, the provider of Pornhub, to ensure the measures they use meet their obligations under the Online Safety Act,” the spokesperson said. eSafety encouraged a “layered approach” to age assurance. A friend called recently and, after some casual chatter about life and work, asked if she could borrow $2000 or more if I could afford it. She “hoped” to pay me back $20 a fortnight. And I knew I’d never see the money again. Being squeezed for money by a friend carries a high risk. AFR I’ve also watched her make several dubious financial decisions over the past two decades. She owned a lovely house when we met, but sold it and lived off the proceeds, which has now all been spent. She now lives with her adult son, and has been in and out of casual work for years. While I worry about her, she was about to start paid work again, and I knew family could look after her. I also have my own financial commitments, including school fees and a second teenager weeks away from getting braces.

On the other hand, I have another friend with a sick husband and three kids, and I’ve offered to loan her money anytime. She’s always declined. Stretching the friendship Mixing money with friendship carries a high risk of strain, awkwardness and resentment if repayment fails. Ask Financial expert Melissa Browne, who agreed to loan almost $300,000 to a friend on the proviso that it was for six weeks. The money was intended as a bridging loan for a business. But it took several hard conversations and an agonising two-year wait for the money to be fully repaid. “It was extraordinarily stressful because the money had been set aside for another purpose. I felt so stupid afterwards, but we were good friends, and you trust your friends when they say they will pay you back quickly.”

title: My grandfather built Myer from nothing. The bile of this debate harms all of us
text:

NationalImmigration nation Opinion My grandfather built Myer from nothing. The bile of this debate harms all of us Michael Myer Contributor October 7, 2026 — 3:00pm

October 7, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A little over 125 years ago my grandfather, Sidney Myer, landed in Port Melbourne, penniless and with little English. Escaping the pogroms in tsarist Russia, he came in the hope that this country would offer him the safety, freedom and opportunity to begin a new life. Typical of so many immigrants before him and since, he started out with nothing, carting a haberdasher’s trading box on his back and selling door to door until he was able to open his first store in Bendigo in 1900. From there, he built the largest department store chain in the southern hemisphere by the time he died in 1934. The original Myer shop in Bendigo in 1905. Sidney Myer is pictured third from left. As the grandson of one of Australia’s most famous and most successful immigrants, it feels like my duty to make an intervention into the debate around the significance of immigration in the cultural, social and economic fabric of this country. As we watch the rise of populism in this country in the form of the One Nation Party, and its leader, Pauline Hanson, what seems to be lost is the profound contribution that immigrants have made, and will continue to make, to the strength and vibrancy of our nation if they are given the chance.

Advertisement

Sidney Myer’s deep commitment to this land that gave him a new home inspired him to build tirelessly and never stop giving back to those in need. This is best exemplified by the work he did funding the construction of Yarra Boulevard that kept hundreds of men employed during the Great Depression, and a massive Christmas dinner he held for the unemployed at the Melbourne Exhibition Centre in 1930 that drew more than 11,000 people across five separate sittings. Retailer and immigrant Sidney Myer. What drove him was the tireless entrepreneurial energy that also spurred so many of this country’s great entrepreneurial immigrants. Men such as Frank Lowy, Dick Pratt, Harry Triguboff and Maha Sinnathamby, who share that same energy. Together they helped shaped the culture, and the social and economic fabric of this country. Through their endeavours they have contributed hundreds of thousands of jobs, and their personal philanthropy has made further enduring impacts on the cultural and social landscape of our nation. What the increasingly strident populist voices being led by One Nation and its openly racist leader Pauline Hanson are doing is demonising, devaluing and degrading the timeless value that immigration and immigrants bring. Just some of the abhorrent comments she has made over the years include that we are “being swamped by Asians”, and that “Islam is a disease … we need to vaccinate ourselves against”. Now she wants to close the door to international students and to the families of skilled migrants.

Advertisement

The Coalition has followed, promising it would deliver “the biggest cut to immigration in the history of this country”. Related Article Opinion

Immigration nation I am the child of an immigrant. So are 51 per cent of Australians Eryk Bagshaw Investigative reporter In listening to these voices and giving comfort to anti-immigration rhetoric we are turning our backs on the enduring legacies of those great immigrants. In every facet of life – science, medicine, the arts, agriculture, industry, and politics – our lives are enriched by the energy, drive and inspiration immigrants bring to our collective lives. It is time for us to stop giving credence to voices that see immigrants as people taking from us and being a burden upon society, worthy of condemnation and censure. To demonise immigrants is essentially un-Australian. We all are enriched by our multicultural heritage and must resile from the notion of a “monocultural” Australia.

Advertisement

We cannot deny the fact that the tens of thousands who seek to build better lives in this country today, just as my grandfather did 125 years ago, do so with the energy, drive and determination to create new lives. They build businesses, drive innovation and contribute to the cultural, intellectual and social dynamism of this country. It’s undeniable that those who are prepared to take great risks in building anew can do great things. Denigrating immigration demeans the memory of all the immigrants who have gone before and blinds us to the contribution that today’s immigrants make now and will continue to make in the future. Let’s not allow a fear of foreigners to pollute our politics. We are all immigrants in this country. Michael Sidney Myer is the grandson of Sidney Myer. Forrestania Resources has quickly put its stamp on the recently acquired Tampia gold project in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region, tabling a maiden JORC-compliant mineral resource of 4.6 million tonnes grading 1.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 223,300 ounces of the precious metal. The estimate, which employed a 0.5g/t gold cut-off grade, marks a significant first step for Forrestania after acquiring the project from established gold producer Ramelius Resources in September. It immediately bolsters the company’s stated strategy of building a hub-and-spoke operation centred on its newly acquired Westonia Hub, which includes the Edna May gold processing facility. An aerial view of Forrestania Resources’ recently acquired Tampia open pit, previously mined by Ramelius Resources, 75 kilometres south of Merredin in Western Australia. The resource is split between an indicated 2.5 million tonnes at 1.47g/t gold for 118,500 ounces and 2.1 million tonnes at 1.56g/t gold for 104,800 ounces in the inferred category. The Tampia project is no stranger to production. Between 2021 and 2023, Ramelius mined an estimated 3 million tonnes from the open pit at a solid grade of 2.1g/t gold to produce around 201,100 ounces. That ore was trucked around 140 kilometres from Tampia to the very same Edna May plant that now sits in Forrestania’s stable.

Advertisement

‘Forrestania’s strategy of long-term gold production is supported by multiple deposits within haulage distance of infrastructure.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty The project is shaping up as a key plank in Forrestania’s ambitious two-hub production strategy. The company is building a classic hub-and-spoke gold machine, corralling satellite deposits around two processing workhorses – the 2.9-million-tonne-per-annum Edna May plant and the 3.2Mtpa Lake Johnston facility – with both earmarked to fire up in early 2027. Before Ramelius broke ground at Tampia, the project held a resource of 8.2 million tonnes at 1.7g/t gold for 460,000 ounces, highlighting the surprising scale of the original mineralised system. Forrestania’s maiden resource for Tampia effectively defines gold remaining beneath and around the existing open pit. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “This maiden estimate highlights a significant addition to the Forrestania Mineral Resources inventory, providing additional Mineral Resource ounces within trucking distance of the Edna May processing facility. With Tampia located within our newly acquired Westonia Hub, we believe this Mineral Resource will play an important role in Forrestania’s strategy of establishing long-term gold production.” The Tampia project is 75km south of Merredin. Geologically, it lies within the Lake Grace Terrane, part of the ancient almost three-billion-year-old Yilgarn Craton which dominates the southwestern quarter of WA.

Advertisement

Gold mineralisation is hosted in a mafic gneiss unit and occurs as shallow-dipping lode zones between 2m and 20m thick, which are considered amenable to conventional open-pit mining. In simple terms, mafic gneiss refers to a usually ancient, banded, coarse-grained metamorphic rock rich in dark, iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals. Forrestania’s mineralisation model was based on a massive historical drilling database of almost 4500 holes for more than 180,000m of drilling by a succession of owners including BHP, Explaurum and Ramelius. Critically, metallurgical testwork conducted by previous owner Explaurum suggests the ore is free-milling and delivers impressive recoveries. Oxide material demonstrated a gold recovery of more than 96 per cent, while fresh rock returned an average recovery of 91.4 per cent through a conventional carbon-in-leach circuit. The maiden resource at Tampia adds to Forrestania’s already significant two-million-ounce plus global inventory. The tally also includes a 285,700-ounce resource at its Lady Ada and Lady Magdalene deposits in the Forrestania Greenstone Belt, the northern tip of which lies an estimated 100km south of the WA town of Southern Cross. Those deposits have a history of high-grade, nuggety gold, with the old Blue Haze pit at Lady Ada previously producing 27,154 ounces at a stellar average grade of 8.81g/t gold.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.
